Not having seen my lord,
My worried heart is as if drunk.
What to do? What to do?
I truly forget myself often!
"Morning Breeze" (Chén Fēng) has three stanzas,
each stanza has six lines.
133 "No Robe" (Wú Yī)
"No Robe" (Wú Yī),
is satire on the use of troops.
The people of Qín
satirize their lord's fondness for attacking and fighting,
his frequent use of troops,
and his failure to share the people's desires.
How can it be said we have no robes?
I will share my robe with you.
The king is about to raise an army,
let us repair our dagger-axes and spears,
I will share hatred with you!
How can it be said we have no robes?
I will share my undergarments with you.
The king is about to raise an army,
let us repair our spears and halberds,
I will act together with you!
How can it be said we have no robes?
I will share my lower garment with you.
The king is about to raise an army,
Let us repair our armor,
and march together with you!
"Wú Yī" has three stanzas,
each stanza having five lines.
134 "Wèi Yáng"
"Wèi Yáng,"
is about Duke Kāng's remembrance of his mother.
Duke Kāng's mother
was the daughter of Duke Xiàn of Jìn.
Duke Wén encountered the troubles of Lì Jī,
and before he returned, the Qin consort died.
Duke Mù accepted Duke Wén.
Duke Kāng was then the Heir Apparent,
and he gifted and saw off Duke Wén at the north bank of the Wèi River,
thinking of his mother who was not to be seen;
when I see my maternal uncle,
it is as if my mother still exists.
When he ascended the throne,
he composed this poem out of longing.
I escorted my maternal uncle,
saying we would reach the north bank of the Wèi River.
What shall I give him as a gift?
A carriage with yellow-bay horses.
I escorted my maternal uncle,
My thoughts are drawn out.
What shall I give as a gift?
Fine gems and jade pendants.
"Wèi Yáng" (Wei River Bank): two stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
135 "Quán Yú" (The Beginning)
"Quán Yú,"
Is an satire about Duke Kāng.
He has forgotten the former lord's old ministers,
and his dealings with wise men have a beginning but no end.
In my time!
The summer houses were spacious;
but now every meal has nothing left over.
Alas!
Not continuing the beginning?
In my time!
Every meal had four stands of food;
but now every meal is not filling.
Alas!
Not continuing the beginning?
"Quán Yú": two stanzas,
each stanza has five lines.
The state of Qín: ten songs,
Chapter 27,
181 sentences.
*Guó Fēng* (Airs of the States), *Chén Fēng* (Airs of Chen) Twelfth.
136 "Wǎn Qiū" (The Mound of Wǎn)
"Wǎn Qiū,"
is satirical of Duke Yōu.
His lascivious dissipation was befuddled and chaotic,
wandering without restraint.
When you bathe,
upon the Mound of Wǎn!
Truly there is affection,
but no hope!
Kǎn sounds his drum,
below the Mound of Wǎn.
Neither winter nor summer,
he encounters their egret feathers.
Kǎn strikes his earthenware jar,
on the road to the Mound of Wǎn.
Neither winter nor summer,
he encounters their egret plumes.
"Wǎn Qiū" has three stanzas,
each with four lines.
137 *Dōng Mén zhī Fén*
"*Dōng Mén zhī Fén*" (The Elm by the Eastern Gate)
criticizes disorder.
Yōu Gōng was lewd and dissolute, and the influence of
customs caused
men and women to abandon their old occupations,
frequently gathering on the roads,
singing and dancing in the markets.
The elm by the eastern gate,
The *xǔ* oak on Wǎnqiū Hill.
The son of Zǐzhòng,
Wanders beneath them.
On a good day, they gather,
In the southern fields.
They don't spin their hemp,
But wander about in the market.
On a good day, they go,
And depart together in a crowd.
I look at you like the mallows,
And you give me a handful of peppercorns.
"*Dōng Mén zhī Fén*" has three stanzas,
each with four lines.
138 *Héng Mén*
*"Héng Mén"*
is to guide Duke Xī (Xī Gōng).
He is well-intentioned but lacks ambition.
Therefore, this poem was written to encourage and support their ruler.
Beneath the Héng Mén,
one can dwell and linger.
The Mì River flows vast and wide,
one can find joy even in hunger.
Must one eat fish,
necessarily from the Yellow River the *fáng* fish?
Must one take a wife,
necessarily a Jiāng girl from Qí?
Must one eat fish,
necessarily from the Yellow River the carp?
Must one take a wife,
necessarily a Zǐ girl from Sòng?
*"Héng Mén"* has three stanzas,
each stanza with four lines.
139 *Dōng Mén Zhī Chí*
*"Dōng Mén Zhī Chí"*
is a criticism of the times.
It criticizes the ruler's licentiousness and foolishness,
and thinking of a virtuous woman to match a gentleman.
The pool by the East Gate,
can be used to soak hemp.
That beautiful and virtuous girl,
can I meet and sing with her?
The pool by the East Gate,
can be used to soak ramie.
That beautiful and virtuous girl,
can I meet and converse with her?
The pool by the East Gate,
can be used to soak rushes.
That beautiful and virtuous girl,
can I meet and speak with her?
"Dōngmén zhī Chí" has three stanzas,
each stanza having four lines.
140 "Dōngmén zhī Yáng"
"Dōngmén zhī Yáng,"
is a satire of the times.
Marriages are out of season,
men and women often go astray.
(Even with) a personal welcoming,
the woman still sometimes does not arrive.
The willow by the East Gate,
its leaves are luxuriant.
Hūn yǐ wéi qī,
míngxīng huánghuáng.
The poplars at the East Gate,
Their leaves are luxuriant. A rendezvous was set for dusk, The bright stars are glistening.
Hūn yǐ wéi qī,
míngxīng zhézhé.
"Dōngmén zhī Yáng" has two stanzas,
Each stanza has four lines.
141 "Mùmén"
"Mùmén" is a satire of Chén Tuó.
Chén Tuó had no good tutors,
Leading him to unrighteousness,
And evils were brought upon the people.
The tomb gate has thorns,
We chop them down with axes.
That man is not good,
The people of the country know it.
They know it but do not stop him,
Who caused it to be so!
The tomb gate has plum trees,
Where owls gather and perch.
That man is not good,
We sing to admonish him.
Gē yǐ xùn zhī. [Singing to admonish him.]
Xùn yǔ bù gù, [Admonishing him, but he pays no heed,]
diāndǎo sī yǔ. [Reverses and misunderstands my thoughts.]
"Mù Mén" èr zhāng, [Two stanzas of "Tomb Gate," ]
zhāng liù jù. [each stanza containing six lines.]
142 "Fáng Yǒu Què Cháo"
"Fáng Yǒu Què Cháo," [“Prevent the Magpie’s Nest,”]
yōu chán zéi yě. [is a lament over slanderous villains.]
Xuān Gōng duō xìn chán, [Duke Xuān greatly trusts slander,]
jūnzǐ yōu jù yān. [causing gentlemen to be worried and fearful.]
Fáng yǒu què cháo, [Prevent the magpie from nesting,]
Qióng yǒu zhǐ sháo. [On the heights grows the fine *sháo*.]
Shuí zhōu yǔ měi, [Who deceives me with flattery,]
xīn yān dāo dāo. [My heart is troubled and anxious.]
Zhōng táng yǒu bì? [In the central hall, are there bricks?]
Qióng yǒu zhǐ yì? [On the heights grows the fine *yì*.]
Shuí zhōu yǔ měi, [Who deceives me with flattery,]
xīn yān tì tì! [My heart is apprehensive and alarmed!]
"Fáng Yǒu Què Cháo" èr zhāng, [Two stanzas of "Prevent the Magpie's Nest," ]
zhāng sì jù. [each stanza containing four lines.]
143 "Yuè Chū"
"Yuè Chū"
is a satire on fondness for beauty.
It speaks of those in positions of power who do not cherish virtue
but delight in beautiful women.
The moon rises, so bright!
A beautiful person, so alluring!
So graceful and slender!
My heart is troubled!
The moon rises, so white!
A beautiful person, so charming!
So leisurely and yielding!
My heart is distressed!
The moon rises, so bright!
A beautiful person, so radiant!
So lithe and graceful!
My heart is grieved!
"Yuè Chū" has three stanzas,
each with four lines.
144 "Zhū Lín"
"Zhū Lín"
is a satire on Líng Gōng.
It speaks of his lusting after Xià Jī,
He gallops forth,
never resting from morning till night.
Why go to Zhū Lín,
following Xià Nán?
It's not to go to Zhū Lín,
or follow Xià Nán!
I harness my team of horses,
and rest in the wilds of Zhū.
I ride my young steeds,
and eat breakfast at Zhū.
"Zhū Lín" has two stanzas,
each stanza with four lines.
145 "Zé Bēi" (The Pond Bank)
"Zé Bēi" is [a poem] criticizing the times.
It speaks of how Líng Gōng and his ministers were dissolute in their state, and men and women
mutually seduced each other,
causing worry, sorrow, and heartbreak.
On the bank of that pond,
there are cattails and lotus.
There is a beautiful person,
how saddened they are!
Awake or asleep, they can do nothing,
Tì sì pāngtuó! (Tears and mucus flow profusely!)
Bǐ zé zhī bēi, (On the banks of that marsh,)
yǒu pú yǔ jiān. (there are cattails and orchids.)
Yǒu měi yīrén, (There is a beautiful person,)
shuò dà qiě juǎn: (tall and handsome:)
wù mèi wú wéi, (awake and asleep, doing nothing,)
zhōngxīn juānjuān! (heart full of sorrow!)
Bǐ zé zhī bēi, (On the banks of that marsh,)
yǒu pú hàndàn. (there are cattails and lotus.)
Yǒu měi yīrén, (There is a beautiful person,)
shuò dà qiě yǎn: (tall and dignified:)
wù mèi wú wéi, (awake and asleep, doing nothing,)
zhǎnzhuǎn fú zhěn. (tossing and turning in bed.)
"Zé Bēi" three stanzas,
each stanza six lines.
The "Chén Guó" section has ten poems,
twenty-six stanzas,
one hundred and twenty-four lines.
Guófēng, "Huì Fēng," thirteenth.
146 "Gāo Qiú"
"Gāo Qiú,"
a high official left his ruler because of his lack of principle.
The state was small and oppressed,
and the ruler did not employ the Way.
He delights in keeping his clothes clean,
leisurely wandering and feasting,
yet he cannot exert himself in matters of governance.
Therefore, this poem was written.
Wearing a lambskin coat, he strolls leisurely;
wearing a fox-fur coat, he attends court.
How could I not think of you?
My heart is troubled and anxious.
Wearing a lambskin coat, he flits about;
wearing a fox-fur coat, he is in the hall.
How could I not think of you?
My heart is filled with sorrow!
His lambskin coat is as glossy as ointment;
when the sun rises, it gleams brightly.
How could I not think of you?
My heart is filled with grief!
"Gāo Qiú" has three stanzas,
each stanza having four lines.
147 "Sù Guān"
"Sù Guān" (Plain Cap) is
a satire on the inability to maintain mourning for three years.
I long to see the plain cap,
The thorny people, so numerous,
Láoxīn tuántuán xī.
If only I could see the plain white garments,
my heart is filled with sorrow,
let me but return home with you!
If only I could see the plain white apron,
my heart is knotted with grief,
let me but be as one with you!
"Plain Cap," three chapters,
each chapter three lines.
148 "There is *chángchǔ* in the Marshy Ground"
"There is *chángchǔ* in the Marshy Ground":
An expression of dislike for excess.
The people of the state disliked their ruler's excessive indulgence
and yearned for someone without desires.
In the damp lowlands grows the *chángchǔ*,
its branches are gracefully bending.
Its young shoots are luxuriant;
happy are you who have no knowledge!
In the damp lowlands grows the *chángchǔ*,
its blossoms are gracefully bending.
Its young shoots are luxuriant;
happy are you who have no family!
In the damp lowlands grows the *chángchǔ*,
its fruit is gracefully bending.
Luxuriant is its loveliness,
Rejoicing at your being without a home!
"Xí yǒu cháng chǔ" has three stanzas,
Each stanza has four lines.
149 "Fěi fēng"
"Fěi fēng,"
Is thinking of the ways of Zhōu.
The state being small and the government chaotic,
He worries about calamity and disaster,
And thus thinks of the ways of Zhōu.
The rushing wind rises,
The rushing chariots are numerous.
I turn and look at the ways of Zhōu,
And my heart is distressed!
The rushing wind blows,
The rushing chariots are swift.
I turn and look at the ways of Zhōu,
And my heart is sorrowful!
Who can cook the fish?
Pour water into the pot and tripod.
Who will return to the west?
Cherish the good news!
"Fěi fēng" has three stanzas,
Each stanza has four lines.
The Guo Feng of the State of Cáo: Four poems,
twelve stanzas,
forty-five lines.
Guo Feng and Cáo Fēng, fourteenth.
150 "Fú Yóu" (Mayfly)
"Fú Yóu" (Mayfly):
A satire on extravagance.
Zhāo Gōng's state was small and constrained,
he had no way to protect himself,
he loved extravagance and trusted petty men,
he would have nothing to rely on.
Mayfly wings!
Fine and neat robes!
My heart is worried,
where is my home?
Mayfly wings!
Brightly colored clothes!
My heart is worried,
where is my rest?
Mayfly digging its burrow,
linen clothes as white as snow!
My heart is worried,
where is my repose?
"Fú Yóu" (Mayfly): Three stanzas,
four lines per stanza.
151 "Hòurén"
"Hòurén"
is a satire on being close to petty men.
Gònggōng distanced himself from gentlemen and favored being close to petty men.
Those watchmen there,
why are they carrying spears and *duì*?
Those men,
three hundred with red knee-covers?
The pelican is on the weir,
not wetting its wings?
Those men,
their attire does not match their virtue.
The pelican is on the weir,
not wetting its beak?
Those men,
they do not achieve their unions!
Luxuriant and dense,
the Southern Mountain rises at dawn.
Gentle and lovely,
the young woman is starving!
"Hòurén" has four stanzas,
each with four lines.
152 "Shījiū"
"Shī Jiū" (The Turtle Dove)
is a satire on inconsistency.
Those in positions of authority are without men of virtue,
because their hearts are not consistent.
The turtle dove is in the mulberry tree,
its chicks are seven.
The good and virtuous man!
His deportment is consistent.
His deportment is consistent?
His heart is like a knot.
The turtle dove is in the mulberry tree,
its chicks are in the plum tree.
The good and virtuous man!
His sash is of silk.
His sash is of silk?
His cap is of black-and-white silk.
The turtle dove is in the mulberry tree,
its chicks are in the jujube tree.
The good and virtuous man!
His deportment is without error.
His deportment is without error?
He rectifies the four states.
The turtle dove is in the mulberry tree,
Her son is in the hazel thicket.
A virtuous and noble person!
Truly a person of the state.
Truly a person of the state?
Why not live ten thousand years!
"The Cuckoo" has four stanzas,
each stanza has six lines.
153 "The Spring Below"
"The Spring Below,"
(is a poem) of longing for good government.
The people of Cáo resent Gòng Gōng's oppression and harsh treatment of the lower classes,
not allowing them to have their proper place,
and are worried and long for a wise king and virtuous Bó.
Clear is that spring below,
soaking the bundled wolf's tail grass.
I sigh waking from sleep,
thinking of the capital of Zhōu!
Clear is that spring below,
soaking the bundled sweet wormwood.
I sigh waking from sleep,
thinking of the capital Zhōu!
Clear is that spring below,
soaking the bundled yarrow stalks.
I sigh waking from sleep,
thinking of the capital city!
Luxuriant are the millet sprouts,
The dark rain enriches them.
The states all have a king,
The Earl of Xun comforts them.
"Xia Quan" has four stanzas,
Each stanza has four lines.
The state of Cao has four poems,
Fifteen stanzas,
Sixty-eight lines.
State Airs, Airs of Bin, fifteenth.
154 "The Seventh Month"
"The Seventh Month,"
Recounts the royal enterprise.
The Duke of Zhou encountered change,
Therefore he recounted how Hòu Jì, the former duke, influenced and transformed customs,
leading to the difficulty of the royal enterprise.
In the seventh month, the Fire Star declines,
In the ninth month, clothes are given out.
In the first month, the north wind blows fiercely,
In the second month, it is bitterly cold.
Without gown or jacket,
How can we finish the year?
In the third month, we repair plows,
On the fourth day, we lift our feet.
Together with my wife and children,
We deliver food to those southern fields.
The Tián Jùn (田畯) is exceedingly pleased.
In the seventh month, the Fire Star declines.
In the ninth month, we are given clothes.
In the spring days, the sun bestows warmth,
There is the oriole singing.
The women carry deep baskets,
Following those small paths,
Seeking the tender mulberry leaves.
In the spring days, the time passes slowly,
Gathering artemisia in abundance.
The women's hearts are sad,
Almost going home with the Gōng Zǐ (公子)!
In the seventh month, the Fire Star declines.
In the eighth month, the reeds grow tall.
In the silkworm month, we prune the mulberry branches,
Taking those axes and hatchets,
To cut down the distant branches,
And lean against those young mulberry trees.
In the seventh month, the shrike sings,
In the eighth month, we start spinning,
Spinning black and spinning yellow,
My red is very bright,
To make clothes for the Gōng Zǐ (公子).
In the fourth month, the xiùyāo flourishes;
In the fifth month, the cicadas chirp.
In the eighth month, we harvest;
In the tenth month, the leaves fall.
In the first period, we hunt foxes,
Taking those foxes and raccoon-dogs,
To make fur coats for the young masters.
In the second period, we gather together,
Continuing our martial exercises.
We say, "Let's privately keep the young boars,"
And present the large boars to the lord.
In the fifth month, the grasshoppers stir their legs;
In the sixth month, the shājī flap their wings.
In the seventh month, they are in the fields;
In the eighth month, they are under the eaves;
In the ninth month, they are at the door;
In the tenth month, the crickets
Enter under my bed.
We plaster up holes and smoke out rats;
We block the north-facing windows and plaster the doors.
Alas, my wife and children,
We say, "Prepare for the new year,
And come dwell in this house!"
In the sixth month, we eat yù and yù;
In the seventh month, we cook kuí and shū.
In the eighth month, we harvest dates;
In the tenth month, we harvest rice,
For this spring wine,
to assist in long life!
In the seventh month we eat melons,
In the eighth month we cut gourds,
In the ninth month we gather hemp seeds,
We pluck bitter herbs and gather firewood of the stinking cedar,
To feed my farmers!
In the ninth month we build the threshing floor,
In the tenth month we bring in the grain:
Millet, glutinous millet, early rice, and late rice,
Rice, hemp, beans, and wheat.
Ah, my farmers!
Now that our harvest is complete,
We go up and enter upon the service of the palace.
In the daytime you thatch the roofs,
At night you twist ropes.
Hasten your work on the houses,
And then begin to sow the various grains!
In the second month we hew the ice with ringing blows,
In the third month we store it in the ice-houses.
In the fourth month, early in the morning,
We offer a lamb with leeks.
In the ninth month there is keen frost,
In the tenth month we sweep the threshing floor.
With paired cups of wine we feast,
Saying, "We kill the lamb."
We ascend to the public hall,
We raise aloft the rhinoceros horn cup,
Wàn shòu wú jiāng! (May you live ten thousand years without limit!)
"Qī Yuè" (July) has eight chapters,
with eleven lines per chapter.
155 "Chī Xiāo" (The Owl)
"Chī Xiāo" (The Owl),
is about Zhōu Gōng (周公) rescuing the state from turmoil.
Chéng Wáng (成王) did not yet understand Zhōu Gōng's (周公) intentions,
so Gōng (公) composed a poem to send to the king,
naming it "Chī Xiāo" (The Owl).
Owl, owl!
Now that you have taken my young,
do not destroy my nest.
I was kind and diligent,
and felt compassion for my young.
Before the sky becomes overcast and rainy,
I will strip off that mulberry bark,
and carefully repair the windows and doors.
Now, you people below,
perhaps dare to mistreat me.
My hands are busy,
I am gathering chú (荼, a bitter herb),
I am storing grain,
and my mouth is utterly exhausted.
I say I have no home!
My wings are worn and tattered,
My tail is thin and bare.
My nest is perched on high,
Where wind and rain toss it about.
My voice is but a plaintive cry!
"The Owl" has four stanzas,
Each stanza has five lines.
156 "Dōng Shān" (East Mountain)
"Dōng Shān" (East Mountain) is about
the Duke of Zhōu's eastern expedition.
The Duke of Zhōu returned after three years of the eastern expedition,
and he rewarded the returning soldiers.
The high officials praised this,
and therefore composed this poem.
The first stanza
speaks of their completeness.
The second stanza
speaks of their longing.
The third stanza
speaks of their wives and families looking forward to their return.
The fourth stanza
rejoices that men and women can enjoy their lives in due time.
The noble man's treatment of others
is to understand their feelings and pity their toil,
and this is how he pleases them.
Shuō yǐ shǐ mín,
the people forget their death.
Is it perhaps the "Dōng Shān"!
I went to Dōng Shān,
lingering and not returning.
I come from the East,
the fine rain is drizzling.
I say I will return to the East,
but my heart is sad for the West:
make that skirt and clothes,
do not employ soldiers to carry branches.
The wriggling caterpillars,
abundantly are on the mulberry fields;
the solitary sleepers,
are also under the carts.
I went to Dōng Shān,
lingering and not returning.
I come from the East,
the fine rain is drizzling.
The fruits of the naked vine,
are they scattered on the eaves?
Woodlice are in the house,
spiders are at the door?
In the open fields of the deer park,
fireflies gleam and move at night?
They are not frightening,
Ah, how worthy of longing!
I went to Dōngshān,
lingering, not returning.
I came from the East,
the light rain is thick.
The stork cries on the anthill,
the woman sighs in her room:
"Sweep and clean the cramped dwelling,
my husband's expedition is about to arrive!
There are mounds of bitter gourds,
steaming on chestnut firewood.
Since I have not seen you,
it has been three years now!"
I went to Dōngshān,
lingering, not returning.
I came from the East,
the light rain is thick.
The oriole flies,
its feathers gleam?
This girl is going to her marriage,
with yellow dappled horses.
Her relatives tie her wedding sash,
with ninety ceremonies.
Her new life is certainly good,
but what will her old life be like!
"Dōngshān" four stanzas,
each stanza twelve lines.
157 《Pò Fǔ》
《Pò Fǔ》
praises Zhōu Gōng 周公.
A Zhou 周 dynasty official used it to express resentment towards the four states.
"Having broken my axe,
and nicked my square axe.
Zhōu Gōng 周公 campaigned in the east,
the four states submitted in fear.
Pity my people,
truly they are greatly valiant!
Having broken my axe,
and nicked my chisel.
Zhōu Gōng 周公 campaigned in the east,
the four states were transformed.
Pity my people,
truly they are greatly admirable!
Having broken my axe,
and nicked my mattock.
Zhōu Gōng 周公 campaigned in the east,
the four states were subdued.
Pity my people,
truly they are greatly blessed!"
The 《Pò Fǔ》 has three stanzas,
each stanza containing six lines.
158 《Fá Kē》
"Fá Kē" (Cutting an Axe Handle)
praises Zhōu Gōng.
A great officer of Zhōu satirizes the court's ignorance.
"How does one cut an axe handle?
Without an axe, it cannot be done.
How does one take a wife?
Without a matchmaker, it cannot be done.
Cutting an axe handle!
The standard is not far off.
When I meet with these gentlemen,
the biān and dòu vessels are properly arranged."
"Fá Kē" has two stanzas,
with four lines per stanza.
159 "Jiǔ Yù" (Nine Nets)
"Jiǔ Yù" (Nine Nets)
praises Zhōu Gōng.
A great officer of Zhōu satirizes the court's ignorance.
"The fish in the nine nets
are zūn (trout) and fáng (bream).
When I meet with these gentlemen,
they wear gǔn robes and embroidered skirts.
The wild geese fly along the islet,
But my lord returns nowhere.
Place your trust in this woman!
The wild geese fly along the land,
But my lord returns no more.
Place your trust in this woman for the night!
Therefore, there is a ceremonial robe!

With gentle cries the deer call,

I have honored guests,

eating the artemisia of the fields.

I have fine wine;

162 "Sì Mǔ (四牡)"
"Sì Mǔ (四牡)" is

We gallop and drive on,

164 *Cháng Dì*
*Cháng Dì* is a poem for feasting brothers.

The flowers of the *táng dì* tree,

Of all the people now living,
none are like brothers:
In the face of death and mourning,
brothers especially grieve.
The plains and marshes gather,
brothers seek each other.
The wagtail is in the fields?
Brothers help in times of distress.
Whenever there are good friends,
how much more we sigh deeply!
Brothers quarrel within the walls,

Whenever there are good friends,
together there is no resistance.
After the turmoil was settled,

Though there are brothers,

Arranging your *biān dòu* dishes,

Harmonious, joyful, and affectionate.
Wives and children in good accord,

Since the brothers are united,
Harmonious, joyful, and deeply content.
May your household be well-ordered,
May your wife and children be happy.
Is this thoroughly investigated and planned,

The "Cháng Dì" has eight stanzas,

165 "Fá Mù"
"Fá Mù" is,

From the Son of Heaven down to the common people,

The sound of felling trees, ding ding!
The birds sing, ying ying.
They come from the secluded valley,

seeking the voices of their friends.

they still seek the voices of their friends;
how much more should men,
not seek the company of friends?
The spirits will listen to it,
and in the end, there will be harmony and peace.
The sound of felling trees, xu xu!
We strain the wine, there is excellence.
We already have a fat lamb,

Why do you not come?

Oh, brightly swept and cleaned!
The offerings are arranged in eight *gui* vessels.
We already have a fat boar,

Why don't you come and find peace?

The bamboo dishes and wooden stands are being filled,

The people's loss of virtue

If there is wine, filter it for me,

Loudly drum for me,

When I have leisure,

166 "Tiān Bǎo"
"Tiān Bǎo,"

Heaven protects and establishes you,

Making you sincerely generous,

Granting you many increases,

Heaven protects and stabilizes you,

May everything be entirely appropriate,

Send down to you lasting fortune,

Like rivers just arriving,

Auspicious and purified victims are prepared as offerings,

The spirits pity [the people],

like the sun in its rising.

167 "Cǎi Wēi"
"Cǎi Wēi" is about

Leaving no time for leisurely rest,
The reason for the Xiǎn Yǔn 獫狁.

Gathering vetch, gathering vetch!
The vetch is now tough.
Saying, "Let's return, let's return!"
But the year is drawing to an end.

The four steeds move smoothly,

The Xiǎn Yǔn (玁狁) are extremely troublesome!
When I left in the past,

Now that I return,

My heart is filled with sorrow,

168 "Chū Chē (出車)"

is completely abandoned,

*Chē Gōng*
is about Xuān Wáng (宣王) returning to the ways of the past.

externally repel the barbarian tribes,
