prepared weapons and equipment,
and reconvened the feudal lords at the eastern capital.
Thereupon, through hunting, he selected charioteers and foot soldiers.
"Our chariots are already sturdy,
our horses are already well-matched.
The four steeds are strong and large,
let us drive to the east."
"The hunting chariots are already well-prepared,
the four steeds are very strong.
To the east there is abundant grass,
let us drive to go hunting."
"That man is in the hunt,
selecting foot soldiers with loud shouts.
Raising banners and setting up yak-tail flags,
catching beasts at Áo (敖)."
"Driving those four steeds,
The four stallions are strong.
Red knee-covers and bronze shoes,
Their meeting is grand and prolonged.
The thumb-ring and arm-guard are ready,
The bows and arrows are well-tuned,
The archers are all together,
Help me raise the target stand.
The four yellow horses are harnessed,
The two outside horses do not lean.
Not losing their speed,
The arrow is released as if breaking something.
The horses neigh gently,
The pennant banners flutter in the breeze!
The foot soldiers and drivers are not alarmed,
Is it that the great kitchen is not full?
This man is going on an expedition,
There is reputation without noise.
Truly a gentleman!
Showing great accomplishment.
"Chē Gōng" has eight stanzas,
each stanza four lines.
180 "Jí Rì" ("Auspicious Day")
"Jírì" (Auspicious Day),
is about King Xuān of Měi hunting.
He was able to carefully attend to small matters and receive those below him,
and there was nothing he did not do to the utmost to serve his superiors.
On an auspicious day, it was Wù (the fifth day of the cycle),
having already sacrificed to Bó and prayed.
The hunting carriages were already well-prepared,
the four stallions were very strong.
Ascending that great mound,
following its many companions.
On an auspicious day, it was Gēngwǔ (the seventh day of the cycle),
having already selected my horses.
Where the animals gather together,
the does and stags crowd closely.
Following the Qī and Jǔ rivers,
is where the Son of Heaven is.
Looking at that central plain,
its game is abundant and plentiful.
In droves, slowly and deliberately,
some in groups, some in pairs.
Completely lead those on the left and right,
to feast the Son of Heaven!
Having drawn my bow,
having grasped my arrows,
shoot that small piglet,
kill this large rhinoceros.
to entertain guests,
and to offer sweet wine!
"Jírì" has four chapters,
with six lines per chapter.
The "Nán Yǒu Jiā Yú zhī Shí" has ten sections,
forty-six chapters,
and two hundred seventy-two lines.
The third of the "Xiǎo Yǎ Hóng Yàn zhī Shí,"
181 "Hóng Yàn"
"Hóng Yàn"
praises King Xuān (Xuān Wáng).
The people were scattered and separated,
not secure in their dwellings,
but he was able to comfort and bring them back,
restore order,
and peacefully gather them,
so that even the lonely and widowed all found their place.
The wild geese fly,
their wings rustling.
That man is on a journey,
toiling in the fields.
Extending to the solitary people,
pitying these widowers and widows!
The wild geese fly,
gathering in the middle of the marshes.
The man is at the wall,
A hundred walls are all being built.
Although it is laborious,
In the end, it will be a peaceful dwelling!
The wild geese fly,
Their sorrowful cries are loud and clear.
These wise men,
Say that I am laborious;
Those foolish men,
Say that I am displaying arrogance!
"Hóng Yàn" (Wild Geese) has three stanzas,
Each stanza has six lines.
182 "Tíng Liáo" (The Courtyard Torch)
"Tíng Liáo" (The Courtyard Torch) praises King Xuān (Xuān Wáng) and uses it as a warning.
How is the night?
The night is not yet over.
The light of the courtyard torch shines.
The gentleman arrives,
The sound of the bells is jiāng jiāng.
How is the night?
The night is not yet at its end.
The courtyard torch is brightly shining.
The lord has arrived;
The phoenix bells chime sweetly.
What time is it now?
The night is drawing toward morning.
The torches in the courtyard are brightly blazing.
The lord has arrived;
Let us go and see his banner.
"Tíngliáo" has three stanzas,
each stanza having five lines.
183 "Miǎn Shuǐ"
"Miǎn Shuǐ,"
remonstrates with King Xuān.
From the flowing waters of the Miǎn,
They go in their courses to the sea.
Swiftly flies the falcon,
Now flying, now alighting.
Alas, my brothers,
My friends and companions!
None are willing to think of the disorder;
Who is without parents?
From the flowing waters of the Miǎn,
The flow is rushing.
Swiftly flies the falcon,
Flying up and flying around.
Thinking of those who leave no tracks,
rising up and going away.
The sorrow in my heart,
cannot be extinguished and forgotten!
Swiftly flies the falcon,
soaring over the middle hills.
The people's false rumors,
will none punish them?
My friend is reverent,
yet slanderous words arise!
"Miǎn Shuǐ" has three stanzas,
two stanzas have eight lines each,
one stanza has six lines.
184 "The Crane Cries"
"The Crane Cries,"
is an admonition to King Xuān.
The crane cries in the marshes,
its voice is heard in the fields.
The fish dive in the deep,
or are on the islet.
I delight in that park,
where there are sandalwood trees;
beneath them is the fallen bark.
The stones from other hills,
Can be considered wrong.
The crane cries in the marshes,
its voice is heard in the sky.
The fish are in the islet,
some are hiding in the deep.
I delight in that garden,
where there are sandalwood trees;
beneath them are paper mulberry trees.
The stones from other mountains,
can be used to polish jade.
"Hè Míng" has two stanzas,
each stanza has nine lines.
185 "Qí Fǔ"
"Qí Fǔ",
satirizes King Xuān.
Qí Fǔ!
I am the king's claws and teeth.
Why are you turning me over to sorrow?
There is nowhere to settle!
Qí Fǔ!
I am the king's claw-officer.
Why are you turning me over to sorrow?
There is nowhere to stay!
Qí Fù!
Truly not wise.
Why do you involve me in sorrow?
There is the corpse of a mother and cooked food!
"Qí Fù" has three stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
186 "White Foal"
"White Foal" is [a poem where]
a grand master (dàfū) satirizes King Xuān.
Brightly white foal,
it eats the seedlings in my garden.
Tether it, tie it,
so as to prolong this morning.
The person I'm thinking about,
at ease and carefree here!
Brightly white foal,
it eats the beans in my garden.
Tether it, tie it,
so as to prolong this evening.
The person I'm thinking about,
here as a welcomed guest!
Brightly white foal,
rushing here to think.
You dukes and lords,
pleasure and ease without limit.
Be careful of your leisurely enjoyment?
Strive for thoughtful retirement!
Brightly white foal,
is in that empty valley.
A bundle of fresh grass,
that person is like jade.
Do not let your words be like gold and jade,
But have far-reaching thoughts!
"Bái Jū" (White Colt) has four stanzas,
Each stanza has six lines.
187 "Huáng Niǎo" (Yellow Bird)
"Huáng Niǎo" (Yellow Bird) is,
A satire on King Xuān (Xuān Wáng).
Yellow bird, yellow bird!
Do not gather in the valley,
Do not peck at my millet.
The people of this state
Are unwilling to nourish me.
I will turn and return,
Back to my clan!
Yellow bird, yellow bird!
Do not gather on the mulberry trees,
Do not peck at my sorghum.
The people of this state
Cannot be enlightened.
I speak of turning, I speak of returning,
Let me go back to my brothers!
Yellow bird, yellow bird!
Do not perch on the *xǔ* tree,
Do not peck at my millet.
The people of this land
Are impossible to live with.
I speak of turning, I speak of returning,
Let me go back to my uncles!
"Huáng Niǎo" in three stanzas,
Each stanza has seven lines.
188 "Wǒ Xíng Qí Yě"
"Wǒ Xíng Qí Yě,"
Is satire on King Xuān.
I walk in the fields,
Luxuriant are the *chū* trees.
Because of marriage,
I said I would come and live in your home.
You do not treat me well?
Return me to my country!
I walk in the fields,
I said I would gather *zhú*.
Because of marriage,
I said I would come and sleep in your home.
You do not treat me well?
Let's go back!
I go through the fields,
saying I am gathering *fú* plants.
I do not think of the old marriage,
but seek for you a new match.
To be accomplished is not based on wealth,
but only on being different!
"Wǒ Xíng Qí Yě" has three stanzas,
each stanza has six lines.
189 "Sī Gān"
"Sī Gān,"
(is a poem about) King Xuān examining the house.
Pure and clear is the stream,
secluded and deep is Southern Mountain.
Like bamboo shoots in abundance,
like pine trees flourishing.
Elder brothers and younger brothers,
thus show affection to each other,
without acting like wild monkeys to each other!
To continue the line of the ancestress and ancestor,
building a house with a hundred walls,
its door facing southwest.
There they live and there they dwell;
there they laugh and there they talk.
Binding it tightly, *gé gé*,
hammering it firmly, *tuó tuó*.
Where wind and rain are warded off,
where birds and rats are driven away,
where the virtuous man dwells in peace!
Like one standing on tiptoe awaiting wings,
Like an arrow, he will be upright;
Like a bird, he will be alert and strong;
Like a pheasant, he will fly high;
And here the lord will ascend!
Luxuriant is the courtyard,
And the pillars are strong.
The uprights are bright,
The dark corners are resonant,
And here the lord will have peace!
Below, fine mats; above, finer ones;
Then he will lie down in peace.
He lies down, he wakes,
And then he interprets my dreams.
What are the auspicious dreams?
They are bears and grizzlies,
They are small snakes and large ones.
The great diviner interprets them:
"Are they bears and grizzlies?"
They are omens of a boy!
"Are they small snakes and large ones?"
They are omens of a girl!
Then a son is born:
he is laid on a bed,
dressed in robes,
and given a zhāng jade scepter to play with.
His crying is loud and clear,
he will wear crimson knee-covers so bright,
and be the lord of his family and the king!
Then a daughter is born:
she is laid on the floor,
wrapped in swaddling clothes,
and given a pottery spindle whorl to play with.
Let her do nothing wrong, let her be without bad manners,
let her only think of wine and food,
and let her not cause worry to her parents!
"Sī Gān" has nine stanzas,
four stanzas have seven lines each,
and five stanzas have five lines each.
190 "Wú Yáng"
"Wú Yáng"
is about King Xuān's testing of the pastures.
Who says that you have no sheep?
Three hundred is the number of flocks.
Who says that you have no cattle?
Ninety are black-mouthed.
Your sheep come,
Qí jiǎo jíjí. Their horns are closely pressed together.
Ěr niú lái sī, Your cattle come here,
qí ěr shīshī. Their ears are moist.
Huò jiàng yú ē, Some descend to the hills,
huò yǐn yú chí, Some drink at the pond,
huò qǐn huò é. Some sleep, some lie down at ease.
Ěr mù lái sī, Your herdsmen come here,
hé suō hé lì, Wearing raincoats and bamboo hats,
huò fù qí hóu. Some carry their dried provisions.
Sānshí wéi wù, Thirty are reckoned as a herd,
ěr shēng zé jù. Then your sacrifices are complete.
Ěr mù lái sī, Your herdsmen come here,
yǐ xīn yǐ zhēng, With firewood and steaming,
yǐ cí yǐ xióng. With females and males.
Ěr yáng lái sī, Your sheep come here,
jīn jīn jīngjīng, Solemn and careful,
bù qiān bù bēng. Neither missing nor scattered.
Huī zhī yǐ gōng, Waving them with the arm,
bì lái jì shēng! All come and ascend!
Mùrén nǎi mèng: The herdsman then dreams:
zhòng wéi yú yǐ! Many are (turned into) fish!
zhào wéi yú yǐ! The banners are (turned into) kites!
Dàrén zhān zhī: A great man interprets it:
zhòng wéi yú yǐ? Many are (turned into) fish?
Shí wéi fēngnián! Truly it will be a year of plenty!
zhào wéi yú yǐ? The banners are (turned into) kites?
The families are numerous and thriving!
"Wú Yáng" has four stanzas,
each stanza has eight lines.
The "Hóng Yàn zhī Shí" (Odes of the Wild Geese) has ten poems,
thirty-two stanzas,
two hundred and thirty lines.
Minor Odes
The fourth of the Odes of Jié Nán Shān
191 "Jié Nán Shān"
"Jié Nán Shān",
is Jiā Fǔ's satire of King Yōu.
Lofty is that Southern Mountain,
its rocks towering.
Grand is Shī Yǐn,
the people all look to you.
My worried heart is like burning,
I dare not jest or talk.
The state is already completely ruined,
why do you not pay attention?
Lofty is that Southern Mountain,
truly covered in vegetation.
Grand is Shī Yǐn,
why are things not fair?
Heaven is sending down many diseases,
Calamities and disorders are greatly multiplied.
The people's words are not good;
the miseries are such that no end can be put to them!
Grand Master Yǐn!
He is the support of Zhōu.
He holds the scales of the kingdom;
on all sides he sustains it;
he assists the Son of Heaven;
he causes the people not to err.
Unpitying is great Heaven!
It should not thus make our master empty.
If he do not attend to things personally, nor draw near to them,
will the common people believe him?
If he do not question, and do not employ,
let him not deceive the princely men.
Let him deal with the easy, and stop (there);
let him not give occasion to small men for apprehension.
Those insignificant relatives by affinity,
should not be in considerable offices.
Great Heaven is unjust!
It sends down these great disorders.
Great Heaven is unkind!
It sends down these great evils.
If the princely men would arrive (at their duties),
they would cause the people's hearts to be composed.
If the princely men would show their equanimity,
they would keep hatred and anger far away.
Alas, unpitying Heaven!
Disorder has no end.
Every month brings forth
That which causes the people no peace.
My heart is as if drunk,
Who is holding the reins of the state?
Not administering the government oneself,
In the end, exhausting the people!
I yoke those four steeds,
The four steeds with necks bowed.
I look around in the four directions,
Distressed, there is nowhere to which I can gallop!
You are luxuriant in your evil,
Helping each other in your wickedness!
Now at ease, now happy,
As if you were pledging each other in toasts!
Impartial is not Heaven!
Our king is not at peace.
Not correcting his heart,
But instead resenting those who are upright.
Jiāfù made this ode,
To investigate the king's reviling.
To transform your hearts,
So as to cherish the myriad states!
"Jié Nán Shān" has ten stanzas,
Six stanzas have eight lines each,
Four chapters, each with four lines.
192 *Zhēng Yuè* (First Month)
*"Zhēng Yuè"*
is about the grand officer (Dàfū) satirizing King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
In the first month, thick frost descends,
My heart is troubled and wounded.
The people's false rumors,
Are indeed greatly increasing.
Thinking of me alone,
My sorrowing heart is greatly agitated! Alas for my cautious heart,
Worn by anxiety until it itches!
My parents bore me,
Why did they give me this suffering?
It does not start with me,
Nor does it end with me.
Good words come from the mouth,
But harmful words also come from the mouth.
My sorrowing heart grows ever greater,
And thus there is contempt!
My sorrowing heart is solitary,
Thinking that I have no good fortune.
The people are innocent,
Together with their servants.
Alas for us people!
From where shall we obtain good fortune?
Zhān wū yuán zhǐ,
yú shuí zhī wū?
Zhān bǐ zhōng lín,
hóu xīn hóu zhēng.
Mín jīn fāng dài,
shì tiān mèng mèng.
Jì kè yǒu dìng,
mí rén fú shèng.
Yǒu huáng Shàngdì!
Yī shuí yún zēng?
Wèi shān gài bēi?
Wéi gāng wéi líng.
Mín zhī é yán,
nìng mò zhī chéng?
Zhào bǐ gùlǎo,
xùn zhī zhān mèng.
Jù yuē yǔ shèng,
shuí zhī wū zhī cí xióng?
Wèi tiān gài gāo?
Bù gǎn bù jú.
Wèi dì gài hòu?
Bù gǎn bù jí.
Wéi háo sī yán,
yǒu lún yǒu jí.
Āi jīn zhī rén!
Hú wéi huī yì?
Zhān bǐ bǎn tián,
yǒu wǎn qí tè.
Tiān zhī wù wǒ,
rú bù wǒ kè.
Bǐ qiú wǒ zé,
rú bù wǒ dé.
Zhí wǒ chóuchóu,

yì bù wǒ lì! The crow looks around, where does it alight? Whose house is it? Look at that central forest, Gathering firewood and brushwood. The people now are in great danger, Looking at the heavens as though in a dream. If we can but establish order, No one will be able to overcome us. There is the great God on High! Who would dare to hate him? Do they say the mountain is low? It becomes a ridge, it becomes a hill. The people's false words, Will no one punish them? Summon those elders, Question them about interpreting dreams. They all say, "I am wise," But who knows the crow's male from female? Do they say that Heaven is high? We dare not but be respectful. Do they say that Earth is thick? We dare not but tread carefully. Alas! These words of lament, Have order and have backbone. Alas for the people of today! Why are they like vipers and lizards? Look at those hillside fields, How luxuriant and special they are. Heaven shakes us, As if it cannot overcome us. It seeks our laws, As if it cannot obtain them from us. It seizes my enemies, But even this is not my strength!
The sorrow in my heart,
Is as if it were tied in knots.
The correctness of this time,
Why is it so perilous?
The burning fire is just rising,
Can it possibly be extinguished?
The glorious Zōng Zhōu (宗周),
Was destroyed by Bāo Sì (褒姒)?
In the end, lasting regret,
Is further burdened by gloomy rain.
Since the cart is already loaded,
You then discard your support.
Having loaded and transported your load,
Will someone like a "Bó (伯)" assist me?
Do not discard your support,
Add more to your spokes.
Frequently look after your servants,
Lest you drop your load.
In the end, you will cross dangerous places,
Was this perhaps unexpected?
The fish in the pond,
Also cannot find joy.
Though hidden and submerged,
Its brightness is still very clear.
My heart is filled with deep sorrow,
Thinking of the state's tyrannical ways!
They have fine wine there,
And also delicious delicacies.
They harmoniously gather with their neighbors,
Marriages are greatly celebrated.
Thinking of me alone,
My heart is filled with deep concern!
Small indeed, they have houses,
Abundant indeed, they now have grain.
The people today have no good fortune,
Heaven prematurely destroys them.
Fortunate are the rich,
Pitiful are the lonely and alone!
“Zhēng Yuè” (First Month) has thirteen stanzas,
Eight stanzas have eight lines each,
Five stanzas have six lines each.
193 “Shí Yuè Zhī Jiāo” (The Intercalary Tenth Month)
"Shí Yuè Zhī Jiāo" (The Intercalary Tenth Month)
Is a Dàfū's (大夫) satire on King Yōu (幽王).
In the intercalary tenth month, on the first day, Xīn Mǎo (辛卯).
The sun was eclipsed,
Truly a great disgrace!
That moon is dim,
And this sun is dim?
The common people of today,
Are truly in great sorrow!
The sun and moon announce misfortune,
They do not follow their course;
The four states are without government,
Not using their good (men).
That moon is eclipsed,
Then it is (seen as) its norm.
This sun is eclipsed,
What is not inauspicious about it?
Brightly flashing thunder and lightning,
Are neither peaceful nor orderly:
All the rivers are boiling,
The mountain tombs are collapsing precipitously.
High banks become valleys,
Deep valleys become hills.
Alas for the people of today,
Why is there no one to punish them?
Huángfù, the high minister,
Is repeatedly the Minister of Instruction.
Jiā Bó is the steward,
Zhòng Yǔn is the cook.
Zōu Zǐ is the Inner Scribe,
Jué is the master of the horse.
Yǔ is the tutor,
The beautiful wives fan the fire in their proper places!
Ah, this Huángfù!
Can it be said that it is not the time?
Why do you make me (suffer)?
Not immediately consulting me?
Tearing down my walls and houses,
The fields are completely overgrown with weeds.
Yuē yú bù qiāng, Saying, "I will not harm anyone,"
Lǐ zé rán yǐ! And behaving in such a ritualistic way!
Huángfǔ kǒng shèng! Huángfǔ is exceedingly wise!
Zuò dū yú Xiàng. He builds the capital in Xiàng.
Zé sān yǒu shì, Selecting the three ministers who have affairs,
Dǎn hóu duō cáng! Indeed, the nobles hoard much!
Bù yìn yí yī lǎo, Unwilling to leave behind even one old man,
Bǐ shǒu wǒ wáng. To guard our king.
Zé yǒu chē mǎ, Selecting those with carriages and horses,
Yǐ jū Cú Xiàng. To reside in Cú Xiàng.
Miǎnmiǎn cóng shì, Diligent in carrying out their duties,
Bù gǎn gào láo. Not daring to complain of hardship.
Wú zuì wú gū, Without crime or guilt,
Chán kǒu xiāo xiāo. The slanderous mouths chatter loudly.
Xià mín zhī niè, The suffering of the common people,
Fěi jiàng zì tiān. Does not descend from Heaven.
Zǔn dá bèi zēng, Whispering and hating behind their backs,
Zhí jìng yóu rén! Competing for position is caused by people!
Yōuyōu wǒ lǐ, My long-suffering village,
Yì kǒng zhī mèi. Is exceedingly afflicted.
Sìfāng yǒu xiàn, All around there is ease,
I dwell alone in sorrow.
The people all indulge in ease,
I alone dare not rest.
Heaven's mandate is not clear,
I dare not imitate
My friends in their self-indulgence!
"Shí Yuè zhī Jiāo" (交) has eight stanzas,
Each stanza has eight lines.
194 "Yǔ Wú Zhèng" (雨無正)
"Yǔ Wú Zhèng" (雨無正)
Is a senior official's lament against King Yōu (幽) of Zhōu (周).
Rain falls from above.
Plentiful as rain,
Yet not fit to be called government.
Vast and expansive Heaven!
Do you not cultivate your virtue?
You send down death, famine,
And military attacks on the four states.
August Heaven displays its anger,
Without thought or plan?
Abandon those who are guilty,
Who have already submitted to their punishment.
But those who are innocent,
Are dragged down to ruin together.
Since the House of Zhōu is destroyed,
where is there a place to stop and rest?
The upright great officers live scattered,
no one knows my toil?
You, great officers of the Three Ministries!
None are willing to work early and late.
You, lords of the states!
None are willing to attend morning and evening.
They said it would be good,
but instead, they repeatedly do evil!
How is it, O vast Heaven!
Your plain words are not believed?
Like one walking far,
then he will arrive nowhere?
All you gentlemen!
Each respect your own person.
Why do you not fear each other,
and not fear Heaven?
Warfare is complete, but they do not retire?
Famine is complete, but they do not cease?
Now I am weary in service,
and daily worn out.
All you gentlemen!
None are willing to use counsel.
When you listen to honest words, you answer,
when you hear slanderous words, you withdraw.
Alas, those who cannot speak!
It is not from the tongue that these things come,
but from the body that one is exhausted.
How clever are those who can speak!
Their glib words flow like a stream,
causing their bodies to be at ease.
Yet what does one say about serving in office?
It is full of anxiety and peril!
If you say they cannot be employed,
you will offend the Son of Heaven (tiānzǐ).
If you say they can be employed,
resentment will reach your friends.
When asked to move to the royal capital,
they say, "I have not yet had a family."
Thinking like a rat, they weep blood;
no words are without fault-finding.
In the past, when you moved out and lived separately,
who helped you build your house?
"Yǔ Wú Zhèng" has seven stanzas,
two stanzas have ten lines each,
two stanzas have eight lines each,
three stanzas have six lines each.
195 "Xiǎo Mín"
"Xiǎo Mín,"
is a great officer (dàfū)'s criticism of King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
The vast heaven sends down its terrors!
Spreading over the lower earth.
Their plans are crooked and perverse;
on what day will they be stopped?
Good plans are not followed;
bad plans are repeatedly used.
When I look at their plans,
they are extremely exhausting.
Full of discordant criticism,
how extremely sad!
When plans are good,
they are all rejected.
When plans are bad,
they are all followed.
When I look at their plans,
where will they end?
My tortoise shells are weary,
they do not tell me what to do.
Planners are extremely numerous,
therefore, nothing is accomplished.
Words fill the court,
who dares take the blame?
As if not planning when traveling afar,
therefore, one cannot find the right path.
Alas for their planning!
They do not follow the example of former people,
nor do they follow the great plans.
They only listen to near-sighted words,
they only contend for near-sighted words.
Like building a house with plans made on the road,
therefore, it cannot be completed!
Though the state has no stability,
it is sometimes wise and sometimes not.
Though the people have no abundance,
some are sagacious, some are planners,
some are reverent, some are regulators.
It is like a flowing spring,
do not let it sink and rot together in failure!
Not daring to bare-handedly assault a tiger,
not daring to wade across the Yellow River.
People know only one thing,
and know nothing about the rest.
Trembling, cautious,
as if facing a deep abyss,
as if treading on thin ice!
"Xiǎo Mǐn" has six stanzas,
three stanzas have eight lines each,
sān zhāng zhāng qī jù.
196 "Xiǎo Wǎn"
"Xiǎo Wǎn",
Is a Daifu's satire of King Yōu.
Listen to the cooing turtledove,
its wings soaring up to the sky.
My heart is sorrowful,
thinking of my ancestors of old.
At dawn, I cannot sleep,
cherishing thoughts of those two persons.
People of complete sagacity,
drink wine and are gentle and restrained.
Those drunkards didn't know,
That each intoxication impoverished them more.
Each of you, respect your manners,
Heaven's mandate will not be given again.
In the central plains, there are beans,
The common people gather them.
The caterpillar has offspring,
The guǒ luǒ wasp carries it away.
Teach your children,
And make them like good people!
Look at those jílíng birds!
Flying and chirping.
Day by day, I am advancing,
And month by month, I am marching on.
Rising early and sleeping late,
Do not disgrace what bore you!
The jiāojiāo sauhuò birds,
Come to the threshing floor to peck grain.
Alas for me, a solitary widow,
Should I be near the shore or in prison?
Holding grain, I go out to divine,
From where comes the sustenance?
Gentle and reverent is this person,
Like birds gathering on a tree!
Anxious and cautious,
As if standing on the edge of a deep valley!
Trembling and fearful,
As if treading on thin ice!
"Xiǎo Wǎn" has six stanzas,
Each stanza has six lines.
197 "Xiǎo Biàn"
"Xiǎo Biàn" is,
A satire of Yōu Wáng.
Written by the tutor of the crown prince.
Those yū birds on their caps,
Fly back and forth in flocks.
The people, none are not prosperous,
I alone encounter misfortune.
What offense have I committed against Heaven?
What sin is mine?
My heart is grieved,
What is to be done?
The Zhou road, once so smooth,
Is now overgrown with dense grass.
My heart is wounded and sore,
Distressed as if being pounded.
I lie down for a moment, then sigh forever,
It is worry that makes me old.
The sorrow in my heart,
Burns like a sick headache!
The mulberry and catalpa trees,
One must treat with reverence.
There is none I look up to who is not a father,
There is none I rely on who is not a mother.
Do I not belong to the downy hair,
Do I not depend on the lining?
Heaven that gave birth to me,
Where is my appointed time?
Luxuriant are those willow branches,
The cicadas chirp ceaselessly.
There is a deep pool,
Thickly covered with reeds and rushes.
Like a drifting boat,
Not knowing where it will reach.
The sorrow in my heart,
Leaves me no time for a brief nap.
The deer run swiftly,
Their feet move nimbly.
The pheasant crows in the morning,
Still seeking its mate.
Like a rotten tree,
Quickly used, it has no branches.
The sorrow in my heart,
Is there no one who knows it?
Xiāng bǐ tóu tù,
shàng huò xiān zhī.
Xíng yǒu sǐ rén,
shàng huò jìn zhī.
Jūnzǐ bǐng xīn,
wéi qí rěn zhī!
Xīn zhī yōu yǐ,
tì jì yǔn zhī!
Jūnzǐ xìn chán,
rú huò chóu zhī.
Jūnzǐ bù huì,
It is not easy to investigate.
The felling of trees is done with hooked tools;
the splitting of firewood is done with axes.
Those who are guilty are let go,
while I am given other things (punishment)!
There is no mountain that is not high,
no spring that is not deep.
The gentleman should not lightly change his words;
ears are attached to the wall!
Do not go over my dam,
do not open my fish trap.
I myself am not spared,
how can I care for my descendants!
"Xiǎo Biàn" has eight chapters,
each chapter has eight lines.
198 "Qiǎo Yán"
"Qiǎo Yán",
is a satire on King Yōu.
A grand master was harmed by slander,
therefore he made this poem.
Oh, vast Heaven!
They say it is like parents.
Without crime or fault,
the chaos is so great.
Heaven has become oppressive!
I am truly without crime.
Heaven is so great and confusing!
I am truly innocent.
At the beginning of the chaos,
usurpation had already begun to take root.
When chaos arises again,
the ruler believes slander.
If the ruler were like one who is angry,
the chaos might quickly be stopped.
If the ruler were like one who is blessed,
the chaos might quickly be ended.
The ruler makes frequent covenants,
therefore chaos is prolonged.
The ruler trusts thieves,
therefore chaos is violent.
Dào yán kǒng gān,
disorder is thereby indulged.
It is not that they merely stop at common things,
but it is a matter of the King's distress!
Majestic are the ancestral temple buildings,
the superior man made them.
Orderly are the great plans,
the sage made them.
Others have thoughts in their hearts,
I can fathom them.
Leaping is the cunning hare,
when it meets a dog, it is caught!
Yielding is the soft wood,
the superior man plants it.
Words that come and go,
in the heart, I count them.
Flowing, copious words,
come forth from the mouth!
Artful words are like a reed pipe,
the face (to utter them) is so thick!
Who is that man?
He dwells by the banks of the Hé River.
Without strength or courage,
his office is a ladder to disorder.
Already insignificant and with a swollen foot,
what courage do you have?
To act presumptuously will be much,
how many are your companions?
"Qiǎo Yán" has six chapters,
each chapter has eight lines.
199 "Hé Rén Sī"
"Hé Rén Sī,"
Sū Gōng satirizes Bào Gōng.
Bào Gōng was a high official,
and he slandered Sū Gōng,
therefore Sū Gōng wrote this poem to sever ties with him.
Who is that person!
Whose heart is so troubled?
Why do you go to my bridge,
And not enter my gate?
Who is it you claim to follow?
Only saying "Bào" follows him?
Two people follow and walk together,
Who caused this disaster?
Why do you go to my bridge,
And not come to comfort me?
The beginning is not like now:
Saying you would not approve of me!
Who is that person!
Why do you go to my Chén,
I hear his voice,
But I do not see his body.
Not ashamed before men,
Not fearing Heaven.
Who is that person!
Who is like a whirlwind?
Why not from the north,
Why not from the south?
Why do you go to my bridge,
Only to disturb my heart?
Your leisurely journey,
Does not even give you time to rest.
Your hurried journey,
Huáng zhī ěr chē? Do you even grease your cart?
Yī zhě zhī lái, When that one comes,
yúnhé qí xū! How angrily he glares!
Ěr hái ér rù, If you return and enter,
wǒ xīn yì yě. My heart will be at ease.
Hái ér bù rù, If you return but do not enter,
fǒu nán zhī yě. Whether it is a refusal is hard to know.
Yī zhě zhī lái, When that one comes,
bǐ wǒ qí yě! He makes me respectful!
Bó shì chuī xuān, The elder brother blows the *xuān* ocarina,
zhòng shì chuī chí. The younger brother blows the *chí* flute.
Jí ěr rú guàn, To be as familiar as stringing together,
liàng bù wǒ zhī? Do you really not understand me?
Chū cǐ sān wù, Bring out these three things,
yǐ zǔ ěr sī! To curse you with this!
Wèi guǐ wèi yù, Turning into a ghost or turning into a water monster,
zé bùkě dé. Then it cannot be obtained.
Yǒu tiǎn miànmù, Having a brazen face,
shì rén wǎng jí? Looking at people without limit?
Zuò cǐ hǎo gē, I make this fine song,
yǐ jí fǎncè! To express my vexation!
"Hé Rén Sī" bā zhāng, "What Sort of Man Is This" has eight stanzas,
zhāng liù jù. Each stanza has six lines.
200 "Xiàng Bó"
"Xiàng Bó",
cì Yōu Wáng yě. is a criticism of King Yōu.
Sì rén shāng yú chán,
gù zuò shì shī yě.
Qī xī fěi xī!
Completing the patterned brocade.
Those slanderous people,
are indeed very excessive!
Wide and extravagant!
Forming the Southern Dipper.
Those slanderous people,
with whom do they consult?"
"Bustling and flitting about!
Plotting to slander others.
Be careful of your words!
They say you are not trustworthy."
"Quick and restless!
Plotting to slander with words.
Will you not receive the consequences?
Soon their schemes will be moved!"
"Treating the arrogant well,
treating the hardworking carelessly.
Azure Heaven, Azure Heaven!
Look upon those arrogant people,
and pity these hardworking people!
Those slanderous people,
with whom do they consult?
Take those slanderous people,
and throw them to the jackals and tigers!
The jackals and tigers won't eat it,
so throw it to the north!
The north won't accept it,
so throw it to the vast heavens!
The road of the Yáng Yuán gardens
meanders at the grave mounds.
The eunuch Mèngzǐ
composed this poem.
All you gentlemen,
respectfully listen to it!
The "Xiàng Bó" has seven chapters,
four chapters with four lines each,
one chapter with five lines,
one chapter with eight lines,
and one chapter with six lines.
The "Jié Nán Shān zhī Shí" has ten sections,
seventy-nine chapters,
and five hundred and fifty-two lines.
Lesser Odes
The Gǔ Fēng Decade, Fifth
201 "Gǔ Fēng"
"Gǔ Fēng"
satirizes King Yōu.
The customs of the world have become decadent,
and the way of friends has been severed.
The sighing valley wind,
Brings wind and rain.
With fear and trembling,
You and I were together.
When settled and happy,
You turn and abandon me!
The sighing valley wind,
Brings wind and whirlwind.
With fear and trembling,
You placed me in your bosom.
When settled and happy,
You abandon me as if forgotten!
The sighing valley wind,
Makes the mountains tall and steep.
No grass but dies,
No tree but withers.
You forget my great virtue,
And think of my petty grievances!
"Gǔ Fēng" (Valley Wind) has three stanzas,
Each stanza has six lines.
202 "Liǎo É" (Luxuriant Artemisia)
"Liǎo É,"
A satire on King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
The people are weary and suffering,
And filial sons cannot complete their nurturing of their parents.
Liǎo liǎo zhě é?
It is not *é*, it is artemisia.
Alas, my parents!
In giving birth to me, they toiled so hard.
Luxuriant is the *é* plant?
It is not *é*, it is *wèi*.
Alas, my parents!
In giving birth to me, they became weary.
The pitcher is empty,
The wine jar feels shame.
The life of an orphan,
Is not as good as a long death!
Without a father, whom shall I rely on?
Without a mother, what shall I depend on?
When I go out, I carry sorrow,
When I enter, I have nowhere to go!
Father, you gave me life,
Mother, you nurtured me,
You stroked me, you fed me,
You raised me, you educated me,
You looked after me, you clothed me,
Coming and going, you carried me.
Wishing to repay your kindness,
Vast Heaven knows no limit!
The Southern Mountain is rugged,
Piāofēng fāfā.
Mín mò bù gǔ,
wǒ dú hé hài?
Nánshān lǜlǜ,
piāofēng fúfú.
Mín mò bù gǔ,
wǒ dú bù zú!
"Liǎo É" liù zhāng,
sì zhāng zhāng sì jù,
èr zhāng zhāng bā jù.
203 "Dà Dōng"
"Dà Dōng,"
a satire on disorder.
The eastern states, burdened by labor and harmed in their wealth,
Dàfū Tán made this poem to express his distress.
There are heaped baskets of cooked food,
there are bent thorn spoons.
The Zhou road is like a whetstone,
its straightness like an arrow.
It is where the gentlemen walk,
and what the common people watch.
I turn my eyes and look at it,
and tears flow down in streams!
Little East, Great East!
The looms are empty!
Twisted hemp sandals,
can they tread on frost?
A frivolous young lord,
walks on the broad road.
Going and coming,
causes me heart-ache!
There is clear Jiu spring,
do not soak the gathered firewood.
Sadly I wake and sigh,
I grieve for those in dread!
Firewood is gathered firewood,
yet it can be loaded.
I grieve for those in dread,
yet they can be given rest!
The sons of the eastern people,
hold their posts laboriously but do not come forward?
The sons of the western people,
how bright are their clothes!
The sons of the boat people,
bear and brown bear are their fur robes?
The sons of private men,
are tried in all the offices?
Some use their wine;
and do not use their gruel?
Richly ornamented is the pendant girdle;
but they do not use their (other) adornments?
Truly in the heavens is the Han River!
Is its light also to be observed?
Look at that Zhīnǚ,
all day going back and forth seven times?
Even though she goes back and forth seven times,
she cannot complete any embroidery?
Look at that bright Qiānniú,
he is not used to load the cart?
In the east there is Qǐmíng,
in the west there is Chánggēng?
There is also the bent Tiānbì,
repeatedly displaying its course?
In the south there is Jī!
It cannot be used for winnowing?
In the north there is Dǒu!
It cannot be used to ladle wine?
In the south there is Jī!
It only flares out its tongue?
In the north there is Dǒu!
The handle points to the west?
"Dà Dōng" has seven stanzas,
each stanza has eight lines.
204 "Sì Yuè"
"Sì Yuè",
is a poem in which a high official rebukes King Yōu.
Those in power are greedy and cruel,
the lower states accumulate misfortune,
resentment and disorder arise together.
In the fourth month, it is truly summer,
in the sixth month, the heat departs.
Our ancestors were not such men,
how could they bear to endure this for me?
The autumn days are bleak and cold,
all the plants are withered and failing.
The disorder and suffering are extreme!
Where is the proper place to return to?
The winter days are intensely cold,
the whirling wind blows fiercely.
The people have none to provide for them,
why am I alone exempt from harm?
On the mountains are fine plants,
the *hóulì* and *hóuméi* plums.
I am abandoned and made a criminal,
no one knows the cause of my offense!
Look at that flowing spring water,
sometimes clear, sometimes muddy.
I daily create misfortune,
how can I be well and provided for?
The overflowing Jiāng Hàn rivers,
are the boundary of the southern states.
I exhaust myself in service,
is there no one who considers me?
Not a quail, not a kite,
yet I fly up to Heaven!
Not a sturgeon, not a *wěi* fish,
qián táo yú yuān! Fleeing and escaping to the deep pool!
shān yǒu jué wēi, On the mountains grow bracken and osmund.
xí yǒu qǐ yí. In the marshes grow boxthorn and elm.
jūnzǐ zuò gē, The gentleman makes a song,
wéi yǐ gào āi! Just to express his sorrow!
“Sì Yuè” bā zhāng, "Sì Yuè" has eight stanzas,
zhāng sì jù. Each stanza has four lines.
205 "Běi Shān" 205 "Běi Shān" (North Mountain)
"Běi Shān", "Běi Shān",
dàfū cì Yōu Wáng yě. is a criticism by a senior officer against King Yōu.
yìshǐ bù jūn, The labor demands are uneven,
jǐ láo yú cóngshì, I toil away at my duties,
ér bùdé yǎng qí fùmǔ yān. yet am unable to support my parents.
zhì bǐ Běi Shān, I ascend that North Mountain,
yán cǎi qí qǐ. claiming to gather boxthorn.
xié xié shìzǐ, These carefree scholars,
zhāo xī cóngshì. toil from morning till night.
wáng shì mí gǔ, The king's affairs never cease,
yōu wǒ fùmǔ! worrying my parents!
pǔ tiān zhī xià, Under the vast sky,
mò fēi wáng tǔ. there is no land that is not the king's.
shuài tǔ zhī bīn, On the edge of the land,
mò fēi wáng chén. there is no one who is not the king's subject.
dàfū bù jūn, The duties of the senior officers are uneven,
wǒ cóngshì dú xián! I alone am virtuous in my toil!
The four steeds go with a rush,
The king’s business is extensive.
I am glad I am not yet old:
My vigour is still coming forth;
My strength is still robust;
I exert myself in all quarters.
Some find rest and repose;
Some exhaust their strength in the service of the state;
Some lie down and sleep on their beds;
Some never cease marching.
Some do not know the call to battle;
Some are miserably toiling.
Some abide in retirement at ease;
Some are busy with the king's affairs.
Some are deeply enjoying their drink;
Some are miserably dreading blame;
Some go out and in, giving counsel freely;
Some do everything that has to be done.
"Běi Shān" has six stanzas,
Three stanzas have six lines each,
Three stanzas have four lines each.
206 "Wú Jiāng Dà Chē"
"Wú Jiāng Dà Chē" (Do Not Push the Big Cart) is about a senior official regretting employing petty people.
Do not push the big cart!
You'll only cover yourself in dust!
Do not think of a hundred worries!
You'll only weary yourself!
Do not push the big cart!
The dust is all murky.
Do not think of a hundred worries!
You won't escape from the outskirts!
Do not push the big cart!
The dust is all thick.
Do not think of a hundred worries!
You'll only burden yourself!
"Wú Jiāng Dà Chē" has three stanzas,
with four lines each.
207 "Xiǎo Míng" (Little Bright)
"Xiǎo Míng" is about
a senior official regretting serving in a chaotic age.
Bright, bright is High Heaven,
Illuminating and overseeing the land below.
I set out on a journey westward,
Reaching the remote wilderness.
In the auspicious days of the second month,
I departed, leaving behind the cold and heat.
The sorrow in my heart,
Its pain is greatly bitter.
Thinking of those fellows together,
My tears fall like rain.
How could I not long to return?
I fear this net of crime!
When I departed in the past,
the months and days were just beginning to pass.
When will I return?
The year is drawing to a close!
Thinking of myself alone,
my tasks are exceedingly many.
The sorrow in my heart,
I fear I have no leisure.
Thinking of those comrades,
anxiously and fondly I think of them.
How could I not long to return?
I fear this reprimand and anger!
When I departed in the past,
the months and days were just beginning to deepen.
When will I return?
Government affairs grow ever more pressing!
The year is drawing to a close,
gathering xiāo and harvesting beans.
The sorrow in my heart,
I bring this suffering upon myself.
Thinking of those comrades,
We rise and leave our lodging.
How could we not long to return?
We fear this fickleness!
Alas, you gentlemen!
You have no lasting, peaceful dwelling.
Quietly attend to your positions,
Uprightness is what you should associate with.
The spirits will listen to you,
And greatly bless you!
Alas, you gentlemen!
You have no lasting, peaceful rest.
Quietly attend to your positions,
Cherish this uprightness.
The spirits will listen to you,
And bestow on you great blessings!
"Xiǎo Míng" has five stanzas,
Three stanzas have twelve lines each,
Two stanzas have six lines each.
208 "Gǔ Zhōng"
"Gǔ Zhōng" (Drums and Bells),
Is a satire on King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
The drums and bells sound loudly,
The Huái River flows vast and rushing,
My heart is worried and wounded.
The virtuous lord,
keeps his promises and does not forget!
The drums and bells sound harmoniously,
the Huái River flows gently,
my heart is filled with sorrow.
The virtuous lord,
his virtue does not falter!
The drums and bells are struck with the large drum,
the Huái River has three islets.
My heart is filled with anxiety.
The virtuous lord,
his virtue is without equal!
The drums and bells ring loudly,
the zithers and lutes are played,
the pipes and sounding stones are in unison.
With "Yǎ" hymns and "Nán" airs,
and with "yuè" dances, nothing is amiss!
"Gǔ Zhōng" has four stanzas,
each stanza has five lines.
209 "Chǔ Cí"
"Chǔ Cí,"
is a criticism of King Yōu.
The government is vexatious and taxes are heavy,
fields and fallow lands are mostly barren,
famine descends and mourning spreads,
the people ultimately flee and perish,
When sacrifices are not accepted,
therefore the gentleman reflects on the past.
Luxuriant are the tribulus plants,
speaking of removing their thorns.
What was done in the past?
I planted millet and sorghum.
My millet grew abundantly,
my sorghum flourished vigorously.
My granaries are already full,
my stacks are truly numerous.
These are used for wine and food,
to offer and to sacrifice,
to appease and to assist,
to seek great blessings!
Numerous and orderly,
we purify our cattle and sheep,
to go and offer the winter and autumn sacrifices.
Some skin and some boil,
some display and some offer.
The *zhù* (祝) prays at the ancestral temple,
the sacrificial affairs are perfectly clear.
Our ancestors are magnificent,
the protecting spirits accept the offerings,
the filial descendant has cause for celebration,
rewarded with great blessings,
longevity without limit!
Those handling the cooking stoves move busily,
The sacrificial stands are large,
Some roasted, some grilled.
The lord's wives are demure,
The dishes are very plentiful.
For guests and visitors,
Offerings and toasts are exchanged.
The rituals are fully measured,
Laughter and conversation are fully enjoyed.
The spirits are thereby reached:
They repay with great blessings,
And unending longevity is given!
Our fire is very hot!
Following the rituals, there are no faults.
The chief invoker delivers the announcement,
Bestowing rewards on the filial descendant,
The fragrant filial sacrifice,
The spirits delight in the food and drink.
Divining for you a hundred blessings,
In the proper measure and manner.
Having purified the millet and sorghum,
Having straightened and disciplined.
May you be granted your utmost limit,
For myriad years, for countless years!
The rituals are fully prepared,
The bells and drums are fully arrayed.
The filial descendant goes to his place,
The chief invoker delivers the announcement:
The spirits are fully drunk and stop,
The royal impersonator is raised aloft.
Drums and bells escort the impersonator,
The divine protectors quickly return.
All the stewards and the lord's wives,
Remove the offerings without delay.
All the paternal uncles and brothers,
Fully discuss matters of private feasting.
The musical instruments are brought in to perform,
In order to secure future blessings.
Your meat offerings are already presented,
Let no one complain, but all rejoice.
Having become drunk and sated,
The small and great bow their heads.
The spirits relish the food and drink,
May they grant you, lord, long life.
Being greatly kind and timely,
May you exhaust them.
Sons and grandsons,
Do not abandon leading them!
"Chǔ Cí" has six stanzas,
Each stanza has twelve lines.
210 "Xìn Nán Shān"
"Xìn Nán Shān,"
Is a satire on Yōu Wáng.
He was unable to cultivate and complete the work of Chéng Wáng,
To survey and govern the land under Heaven,
in order to carry on the achievements of Yǔ [Yǔ] the Great,
therefore the superior man reflects on antiquity.
Truly, that Southern Mountain,
was cultivated by Yǔ [Yǔ].
The cultivated fields and damp lowlands,
are farmed by his great-grandsons.
We survey and govern,
with the fields facing south and east.
In the heavens, gathering clouds,
falling snow thick and fast.
Adding to it fine, drizzling rain,
abundant and rich,
soaking and saturating,
producing for me all kinds of grains.
The borders of the fields extend evenly,
the millet and sorghum grow luxuriantly.
The harvest of the great-grandsons,
is used for wine and food.
Presented to our representative of the deceased and guests,
may they live long and prosper!
In the middle of the fields are huts,
at the borders of the fields are melons.
They are peeled and pickled,
and offered to our great ancestors.
May my great-grandsons live long and enjoy abundant years,
Receiving blessings from Heaven!
We offer pure wine in sacrifice,
Accompanied by a red bull,
To honor our ancestors:
We hold the luan-adorned knife,
To open its hide,
And take its blood and fat.
We offer and sacrifice this,
With rich and fragrant aroma,
The sacrificial rites are perfectly bright.
Our ancestors are majestic:
May they requite us with great blessings,
Boundless longevity!
The "Xìn Nán Shān" has six stanzas,
Each stanza containing six lines.
The "Gǔ Fēng zhī Shí" has ten poems,
Fifty-four stanzas,
Three hundred and fifty-six lines.
Minor Odes
The Sixth of the Fǔ Tián Decade
211 "Fǔ Tián"
"Fǔ Tián" (Great Fields),
Is an satire of King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
The virtuous person laments the present and thinks of the past.
Broad is that large field,
yearly yielding ten thousand sheaves.
I take of its stored grain,
to feed my farmers,
from ancient times there have been harvests.
Now I go to the southern fields,
some weeding, some hoeing,
the millet and sorghum growing luxuriantly.
Here and there they rest,
feasting my brave officers.
With my cleansed offerings,
and my sacrificial sheep,
to the god of the soil and the spirits of the four directions.
My fields are now in good condition,
the joy of the farmers.
With zithers and drums sounding,
to welcome the ancestor of agriculture (Tiánzǔ).
To pray for sweet rain,
to bless my millet and sorghum,
to nourish my men and women.
The great-grandson comes here!
With his wife and children,
bringing food to those in the southern fields,
the field officer (Tiánjùn) is greatly pleased.
They push aside what's around them,
Taste whether it's delicious or not.
The grain is easily grown in long acres,
In the end, it is good and plentiful.
The great-grandson is not angry,
The farmers are truly diligent.
The great-grandson's crops
Are like thatch and like beams.
The great-grandson's granaries
Are like mounds and like hills.
Then they seek thousands of granaries,
Then they seek ten thousands of storehouses.
Millet, broomcorn millet, rice, and glutinous millet
Are the farmers' joy.
They are rewarded with great blessings,
Boundless longevity!
"Fǔ Tián" (Vast Fields), four stanzas,
Each stanza ten lines.
212 "Dà Tián" (Great Fields)
"Dà Tián" (Great Fields)
Is a criticism of King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
It speaks of widows and widowers being unable to support themselves.
The great fields are rich with crops:
Having sown and prepared,
Having made everything ready, then they begin their work,
Yǐ wǒ qín sì,
chù zài nán mǔ.
Bō jué bǎi gǔ,
jì tíng qiě shuò,
zēngsūn shì ruò.
The seeds are now square and black,
Now they are firm and good,
There is no darnel and no weeds.
We drive away the borers,
And also the grubs and the weevils.
Let them not harm our young crops!
The God of the Fields is divine,
Seize them and give them to the blazing fire!
There are thick clouds rising,
Sending down abundant rain.
It rains on our public fields,
And then reaches our private ones.
In those fields there are young crops unharvested,
In these fields there are sheaves ungathered;
In those fields are scattered handfuls,
In these fields are lingering ears:
All this is the profit of the widow!
Let our great-grandchildren come to see this!
Taking their wives and children,
To carry food to them in the southern fields,
The Field Officer will be greatly pleased.
He will come to offer pure sacrifice:
With its reddish-black (ox),
And its millet and sorghum,
We offer and sacrifice,
To seek great blessings!
"Dà Tián" (Great Fields) has four stanzas,
Two stanzas have eight lines each,
Two stanzas have nine lines each.
213 "Zhān Bǐ Luò Yǐ"
"Zhān Bǐ Luò Yǐ" (Gazing at the Luò River),
Is a criticism of King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
It reflects on how ancient, wise kings were able to ennoble and appoint feudal lords,
Rewarding good and punishing evil.
Gazing at the Luò (Luò) River,
The water is so vast.
When the noble one arrives,
Blessings and prosperity will be like thatch.
The brilliant armor is splendid,
With which to raise the six armies.
Gazing at the Luò (Luò) River,
The water is so vast.
When the noble one arrives,
The scabbard and jade ornament are complete.
May the noble one live ten thousand years,
To protect his family and home!
Looking at the Luo River,
its waters are vast.
The lord has arrived,
blessings and prosperity are now shared.
May the lord live for ten thousand years,
and protect his family and state!
"Zhān Bǐ Luò Yǐ" has three stanzas,
each with six lines.
214 "Cháng Cháng Zhě Huā"
"Cháng Cháng Zhě Huā"
is a criticism of Yōu Wáng.
In ancient times, officials' positions were hereditary.
When petty men are in power,
slander and flattery advance together,
abandoning those of virtuous character,
and cutting off the lines of meritorious officials.
The splendid flowers,
their leaves are luxuriant.
I meet this man,
my heart is at ease.
My heart is at ease,
therefore he has a good reputation.
The splendid flowers,
their color is yellow.
I see that gentleman,
How refined and cultured he is!
How refined and cultured he is,
Therefore he has good fortune!
Luxuriant are the blossoms,
Some yellow, some white.
I see that gentleman,
Riding his team of four dapple-gray horses.
Riding his team of four dapple-gray horses,
The six reins gleam sleekly.
To the left, to the left!
He is fit to be a lord.
To the right, to the right!
He possesses the qualities of a lord.
Because he possesses them,
Therefore he resembles one.
"Shāng Shāng Zhě Huā" (裳裳者華) has four stanzas,
Each stanza has six lines.
215 "Sāng Hù" (桑扈)
"Sāng Hù" (桑扈) is,
An satire against King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
Between lord and subjects, superiors and inferiors,
Actions lack propriety and refinement.
Flitting about, the mulberry-pheasants,
Whose wings are bright.
The princely man is happy;
He receives blessing from Heaven.
Flitting about, the mulberry-pheasants,
Whose necks are bright.
The princely man is happy;
He is a screen to all the states.
He is a screen, he is a support;
All the princes take him as their pattern.
Do they not repress themselves? do they not make efforts?
So do they receive much blessing.
The rhinoceros-cups are curved;
The good wine is mild.
Is there no satisfaction in this mutual giving?
All happiness will come to seek them!
"Sāng Hù," four stanzas,
each stanza four lines.
216 "Yuān Yāng"
"Yuān Yāng",
is a satire on King Yōu.
It speaks of how the wise kings of antiquity had a proper way of dealing with all things,
and exercised moderation in their personal support and nourishment.
The mandarin ducks fly about;
Nets are used to catch them.
May the princely man live ten thousand years!
May blessing and emoluments be rendered to him!
Yuānyāng are on the bridge,
They fold their left wings.
May the lord live for ten thousand years!
May his vast blessings be fitting!
The carriage horses are in the stable,
Feed them and groom them.
May the lord live for ten thousand years!
May blessings and prosperity nourish him!
The carriage horses are in the stable,
Feed them and groom them.
May the lord live for ten thousand years!
May blessings and prosperity pacify him!
"Yuānyāng" has four stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
217 "Kuǐ Biàn"
"Kuǐ Biàn" is
a poem by the dukes criticizing King Yōu of Zhōu.
He is tyrannical and without affection,
unable to feast and be joyful with those of the same surname,
or to be intimate and harmonious with his nine degrees of kindred.
He is isolated and endangered, on the verge of ruin.
Therefore, I have made this poem.
There is a cap with flaps!
What is its significance?
Your wine is already delicious,
your dishes are already excellent.
Are they truly strangers?
(They are) brothers, not others!
The dodder and the maidenhair creeper
are attached to the pine and cypress.
Before seeing you, my lord (jūnzǐ),
my heart was heavy with worry.
Now that I have seen you, my lord (jūnzǐ),
perhaps I will find relief and joy!
There is a cap with flaps!
What is the occasion?
Your wine is already delicious,
your dishes are seasonal.
Are they truly strangers?
(They are) brothers, all coming together!
The dodder and the maidenhair creeper
are attached to the pine.
Before seeing you, my lord (jūnzǐ),
my heart was troubled.
Having seen the gentleman,
may we hope for good!
There is a person with the cap cords!
Indeed, it is on his head.
Your wine is already delicious,
your dishes are already abundant.
Are they really strangers?
(They are) brothers, nephews, and maternal uncles!
Like that rain and snow,
first gathers as sleet.
Death and funerals have no fixed day,
we won't see each other for long.
Enjoy the wine tonight,
the gentlemen are feasting!
"Kuǐ Biàn" has three stanzas,
each stanza has twelve lines.
218 "Chē Xiá"
"Chē Xiá,"
a grand officer satirizing King Yōu.
Bāo Sì was jealous and envious,
immoral ways advanced together,
slanderous cunning ruined the state,
and virtuous grace was not extended to the people.
The people of Zhōu desired to obtain a virtuous woman to match with a gentleman,
therefore they made this poem.
Jiānguān chē zhī xiá xī, The rattling of the linchpins of the carriages,
Sī luán jì nǚ shì xī. I think of that lovely Jì Nǚ going away.
Fěi jī fěi kě, Not hungry, not thirsty,
Dé yīn lái kuò. Her virtuous fame comes to encompass (us).
Suī wú hǎoyǒu, Though there are no close friends,
Shì yàn qiě xǐ. Let us feast and rejoice.
Yī bǐ píng lín, Leaning on that level forest,
Yǒu jí wéi jiāo. There are pheasants gathering.
Chén bǐ shuò nǚ, This great lady,
Lìng dé lái jiào. Her excellent virtue comes to instruct (us).
Shì yàn qiě yù, Let us feast and praise,
Hǎo ěr wú shè! Good it is to be without satiety!
Suī wú zhǐ jiǔ, Though there is no fine wine,
Shì yǐn shù jī. Let us drink, perhaps we will get close.
Suī wú jiā yáo, Though there are no fine delicacies,
Shì shí shù jī. Let us eat, perhaps we will get close.
Suī wú dé yǔ nǚ, Though there is no one virtuous to share (this) with me,
Shì gē qiě wǔ! Let us sing and dance!
Zhì bǐ gāo gāng, Ascend that high ridge,
Xī qí zuò xīn. Chop its oak firewood.
Xī qí zuò xīn, Chop its oak firewood,
Qí yè xǔ xī. Its leaves are luxuriant.
Xiān wǒ gòu ěr, Rare it is that I meet you,
Wǒ xīn xiě xī! My heart is at ease!
Gāoshān yǎng zhǐ, High mountains, look up to them;
Jǐngxíng háng zhǐ. Great roads, follow them.
Sì mǔ fēifēi, The four stallions gallop,
The six reins are like a qín.
I meet with you, new bride,
to comfort my heart!
"Chē Xiá" has five stanzas,
each stanza has six lines.
219 "Green Flies"
"Green Flies"
is a poem where a high official satirizes King Yōu.
Buzzing green flies,
land on the fence!
Oh, amiable lord,
do not believe slanderous words!
Buzzing green flies,
land on the thorns!
The slanderers are without limit,
causing chaos in the four states!
Buzzing green flies,
land on the hazel!
The slanderers are without limit,
creating discord between the two of us!
"Green Flies" has three stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
220 "The First Feast for the Guests"
"Bīn Zhī Chū Yán"
is Wèi Wǔ Gōng's satire on the times.
Yōu Wáng was dissolute and negligent, associating closely with petty people,
drinking wine without restraint,
and the whole country was influenced by it.
Lords and ministers, superiors and inferiors,
were all indulging in drunkenness and licentiousness.
Wǔ Gōng, having returned to his state,
then composed this poem.
At the beginning of the feast for the guests,
those on the left and right are orderly.
The bamboo dishes and wooden stands are neatly arranged,
and the dishes of meat and fruit are in abundance.
The wine is already blended and delicious,
and drinking the wine is very harmonious.
The bells and drums have already been set up,
and offering toasts is leisurely.
The large target has already been raised,
and the bows and arrows are drawn.
The archers are all assembled,
come, show your skill,
hitting the target,
to pray for your rank.
With flute dances, reed organs, and drums,
the music is harmoniously played,
to solemnly please our glorious ancestors.
In order to harmonize the hundred rites,
the hundred rites are thus performed.
May you have abundant descendants and prosperity like a forest,
I bestow upon you pure blessings,
may your descendants be immersed in them.
Immersed in joy, it is said to be delightful,
each displays your abilities.
The guests hold up their cups for a toast,
the family members enter and offer more.
Pour from the great bronze cup,
to present in accordance with your proper time.
At the beginning of the guests' feast,
they are gentle and respectful.
Before they are drunk,
their deportment is very proper.
When they are drunk,
their deportment becomes unsteady.
They leave their seats and move about,
repeatedly dancing clumsily.
Before they are drunk,
their deportment is subdued.
When they are drunk,
their deportment becomes unruly.
This is what is called being drunk,
they no longer know their order.
When the guests are drunk,
Zài hào zài náo.
Disrupting my bamboo vessels,
Repeatedly dancing unsteadily.
This is called being drunk,
Not knowing where to stop.
The tilted cap so suddenly,
Repeatedly dancing clumsily.
Having drunk and then leaving,
Together receiving blessings.
Being drunk and not leaving,
Is called diminishing virtue.
Drinking wine is truly good,
Displaying proper demeanor!
In all this drinking,
Some are drunk, some are not.
Having established supervisors,
And assistant scribes.
Those who are drunk behave badly,
Those not drunk feel ashamed instead.
Do not listen to what they say,
Do not allow great negligence.
Things you shouldn't say, don't say them;
Things you shouldn't speak of, don't speak of them.
Words that come from drunkenness,
Are like letting out a young goat.
Three cups and they don't know themselves,
How much more if they dare to drink more!
"Bīn zhī Chū Yán" has five chapters,
with fourteen lines per chapter.
The "Fǔ Tián zhī Shí" has ten poems,
thirty-nine chapters,
and two hundred and ninety-six lines.
The seventh decade of the Lesser Odes, "Yú Zǎo"
221 "Yú Zǎo"
“Yú Zǎo,”
satirizes King Yōu.
It says that all things lose their nature,
the King dwells in Hàojīng,
and will not be able to enjoy himself,
therefore the gentleman thinks of the ancient King Wǔ.
Are the fish in the algae?
They have large heads.
Is the King in Hàojīng?
How can he happily drink wine!
Are the fish in the algae?
They have long tails.
Is the King in Hàojīng?
How can drinking wine be happiness!
Are the fish in the algae?
They rely on the cattails.
Is the King in Hàojīng?
How unrestrained his dwelling!
"Yú Zǎo" (Fish Algae) consists of three chapters,
each chapter containing four lines.
222 "Cǎi Shū" (Gathering Beans)
"Cǎi Shū,"
satirizes King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
He disrespected the feudal lords.
When the feudal lords came to court,
he failed to bestow rewards and appointments according to ritual,
repeatedly summoned them for gatherings,
and lacked trustworthiness;
therefore, a wise man saw these early signs and reflected on the past.
Gathering beans, gathering beans,
with baskets and crates.
The lords come to court,
what shall be bestowed upon them?
Though nothing is given,
carriages and horses.
What more shall be given?
Black robes and embroidered garments.
The gushing spring,
is where they gather celery.
The lords come to court,
to observe the flags.
The flags flutter,
The sound of the luan bells is clear.
With chariot horses and teams of four,
to where the jūn zǐ (君子) arrives.
Red knee-covers at the thigh,
slanted kerchiefs below.
Those crossed ornaments are not loose,
given by the Son of Heaven.
Happy is the jūn zǐ (君子)!
The Son of Heaven commands him.
Happy is the jūn zǐ (君子)!
Blessings and emoluments are extended to him.
Of the Quercus mongolica branches,
its leaves are luxuriant.
Happy is the jūn zǐ (君子)!
He sustains the state of the Son of Heaven.
Happy is the jūn zǐ (君子)!
Ten thousand blessings are shared.
Evenly to his left and right,
they all follow and comply.
The floating willow-wood boat,
with ropes to secure it.
Happy is the jūn zǐ (君子)!
The Son of Heaven relies on him.
Happy is the jūn zǐ (君子)!
Blessings and emoluments enrich him!
How leisurely and carefree!
Also, this is excessive!
"Picking Sow Thistles," five chapters,
each chapter eight lines.
223 "Horn Bow"
"Horn Bow,"
is a satire by fathers and elder brothers directed at King Yōu.
Because he does not cherish the nine branches of his clan but loves slanderous flatterers,
and flesh and blood resent each other,
therefore this poem was composed.
Bright red is the horn bow,
how quickly it is bent back!
Brothers and marital relations,
do not mutually distance yourselves!
If you distance yourselves,
the people will all follow.
If you instruct them,
the people will all imitate.
To treat brothers well,
is truly ample and generous.
Not to treat brothers well,
is to mutually bring about sickness.
The people who are without goodness,
resent each other in one region.
Accepting honors without yielding,
as for oneself, this is ruin!
An old horse instead becomes a colt,
not caring for what comes after them:
Like eating until stuffed,
like taking wine as much as one can.
Do not teach monkeys to climb trees,
like plastering with mud and then attaching it.
The junzi 君子 have fine plans,
the xiǎorén 小人 associate with them.
The rain and snow fall heavily,
seeing the sunshine, it melts.
No one is willing to condescend and give away,
and so they dwell in haughty pride.
The rain and snow drift about,
seeing the sunshine, it flows away.
Like Mán 蠻 and Máo 髦,
this is what I worry about!
"Jiǎo Gōng 角弓" has eight stanzas,
each stanza four lines.
224 "Wǎn Liǔ 菀柳"
"Wǎn Liǔ 菀柳" is,
a criticism of Yōu Wáng 幽王.
Cruel and without kin,
and his punishments are not just,
the zhūhóu 諸侯 all do not want to come to court,
speaking of how the king's affairs were not worth attending.
There are luxuriant willows!
Why not rest beneath them?
God is greatly angered,
do not bring ruin upon yourselves.
Let me bring you peace,
afterwards, I will reach my limit!
There are luxuriant willows!
Why not rest a while?
God is greatly angered,
do not bring exhaustion upon yourselves.
Let me bring you peace,
afterwards, I will depart!
There is a bird flying high?
It also approaches the heavens.
The hearts of those people,
where do they arrive?
Why can't I pacify them,
they dwell with disastrous arrogance?
"Wǎn Liǔ" has three stanzas,
each stanza has six lines.
225 *Dū Rénshì*
*Dū Rénshì*:
A Zhōu dynasty poem satirizing the inconstancy of dress.
In ancient times, those who governed the people,
their clothing was not changed at whim,
their demeanor was composed and consistent,
so as to regulate the people.
Then the people's virtue returned to unity,
grieving that now we no longer see the people of old.
Those gentlemen of the capital,
wear fox-fur coats, yellow and bright.
Their countenance does not change,
their speech is well-ordered.
Will they return to Zhōu?
What all the people hope for!
Those gentlemen of the capital,
wear rush hats with black silk cords.
Those ladies and gentlemen,
their hair is straight and smooth as silk.
If I do not see them,
my heart is not pleased!
Those gentlemen of the capital,
their ears are adorned with jade.
Those ladies and gentlemen,
are called Yǐn Jí.
I do not see her,
my heart is bound in melancholy!
Those people of the capital,
let their sashes hang down and walk with dignity.
Those noble ladies,
their coiled hair is like a scorpion.
I do not see her,
I will then go forth and follow her!
It is not merely that they let their sashes hang down,
their sashes are more than sufficient.
It is not merely that they coil their hair,
their coiled hair is like a banner.
I do not see her,
how can I not gaze longingly?
"Dū Rén Shì" has five stanzas,
each stanza has six lines.
226 "Cǎi Lǜ"
"Cǎi Lǜ,"
is to satirize resentment and widowhood.
In the time of Yōu Wáng, there were many who were resentful and widowed.
All morning I gather green plants,
not filling even a handful.
My hair is tangled and unkempt,
I will just go home and wash it.
All morning long, I gather indigo,
But cannot fill a fold of my skirt.
A five-day deadline is set,
But on the sixth day, it is not yet met.
This man goes hunting,
He says to case his bow.
This man goes fishing,
He says to reel in his line.
What does he fish for?
Bream and dace.
Bream and dace?
How numerous are the onlookers!
"Cǎi Lǜ" has four stanzas,
Each stanza has four lines.
227 "Shǔ Miáo"
"Shǔ Miáo" (Millet Sprouts),
Is a satire on Yōu Wáng.
He could not enrich the world with his kindness,
And the ministers could not perform the duties of Zhào Bó.
Luxuriant are the millet sprouts,
The gentle rain nourishes them.
Slowly I travel south,
Zhào Bó comforts me.
I carry my burdens, I push my carts,
My wagons and my oxen.
When my journey is complete,
I will surely return home!
My foot soldiers and my charioteers,
My officers, my troops.
My journey is now complete,
Surely it may be said, "Let's return to our place!"
Solemnly, the work is completed,
Shào Bó planned it.
Gloriously, the army marched,
Shào Bó brought it to fruition.
The plains and marshes are now level,
The spring flows are now clear.
Shào Bó has accomplished it,
The king's heart is then at peace!
"Shǔ Miáo" consists of five stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
228 "Xí Sāng"
"Xí Sāng" is
an indictment of King Yōu. Inferior men are in positions of authority,
superior men are in the countryside,
longing to see the superior man,
and dedicating their hearts to serving him.
The white mulberry has terraces,
its leaves are abundant.
Now that I have seen the gentleman,
how great is my joy!
The white mulberry has terraces,
its leaves are luxuriant,
now that I have seen the gentleman,
how could I not be happy!
The white mulberry has terraces,
its leaves are dark.
Now that I have seen the gentleman,
his virtuous words are exceedingly good.
My heart is filled with love,
how can I not express it?
In my heart I treasure it,
on what day will I forget it!
"Xísāng" has four stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
229 "Bái Huá"
"Bái Huá,"
the people of Zhōu satirize Queen Yōu.
King Yōu took a woman from Shēn as his queen,
then he obtained Bāo Sì and deposed Queen Shēn.
Therefore, the lower states imitated this,
Taking a concubine as wife,
taking a son of a concubine to replace the rightful heir.
The king was unable to govern it,
so the people of Zhōu 周 wrote this poem about it.
White are the flowers of the *jiān* rush,
white the *máo* grass bound in bundles.
That person is far away,
leaving me alone.
Bright are the white clouds,
dewing those *jiān* and *máo* grasses.
Is the path to Heaven difficult?
That person does not plan!
The *Biāo* pond flows northward,
flooding those rice fields.
Whistling and singing, I wound my heart,
thinking of that great person!
I gather mulberry firewood,
and pile it up by the fire pit.
That great person,
truly troubles my heart!
Drums and bells sound in the palace,
their sound heard outside.
Are you worried about me,
seeing me walking slowly?
There is an egret on the beam,
there is a crane in the forest.
That large person,
truly troubles my heart!
The mandarin ducks are on the beam,
folding their left wings.
This person is not good,
inconstant in virtue.
There is a flat stone,
treading on it, how low!
This person's departure,
makes me ill!
"Bái Huá" has eight stanzas,
each stanza four lines.
230 "Mián Mán"
"Mián Mán"
is a poem by a humble minister satirizing disorder.
The high officials do not use benevolence,
forget the humble and lowly,
are unwilling to feed,
teach, or transport them,
therefore this poem was made.
Gently chirping yellow birds!
Perch on the corner of the hill.
The road is said to be far,
how weary I am!
yǐn zhī shí zhī,
jiào zhī huì zhī.
mìng bǐ hòu chē,
wèi zhī zài zhī.
Softly chirping yellow birds!
Perching on the corner of the hill.
How dare we be weary of marching?
Fearing we cannot keep pace. Drink and feed them,
Instruct and teach them.
Order the carriage behind,
Tell it to carry them.
Softly chirping yellow birds!
Perching on the side of the hill.
How dare we be weary of marching?
Fearing we cannot reach the end!
Drink and feed them,
Instruct and teach them.
Order the carriage behind,
Tell it to carry them.
"Miánmán" in three stanzas,
each stanza with eight lines.
231 "The Gourd Leaves"
"The Gourd Leaves,"
This is a daìfū's criticism of Yōu Wáng.
The ruler abandons ritual and cannot practice it,
even though there are sacrificial animals and ample provisions, he is unwilling to use them.
Therefore, (we) think of the people of ancient times, who did not abandon ritual because of meager offerings.
Fluttering, fluttering are the gourd leaves,
pick them and cook them?
The jūnzǐ has wine,
let us pour and taste it.
There is a rabbit's head,
roast it and bake it?
The jūnzǐ has wine,
let us pour and offer it.
There is a rabbit's head,
bake it and grill it?
The jūnzǐ has wine,
let us pour and pledge toasts with it.
There is a rabbit's head,
bake it and roast it?
The jūnzǐ has wine,
let us pour and return the toasts with it.
"Hù Yè" has four stanzas,
each stanza has four lines.
232 *Jiànjiàn zhī Shí* (Gradually Increasing Rock)
*Jiànjiàn zhī Shí*,
is a poem from the lower states criticizing King Yōu (Yōu Wáng).
The Róng and Dí barbarians rebelled against him,
and the states of Jīng and Shū did not come to court.
Therefore, he ordered generals to lead eastern expeditions,
and the soldiers suffered from prolonged service abroad.
Hence, this poem was written.
Gradually increasing is the rock,
how high it is!
The mountains and rivers are long and far,
how arduous it is!
The warriors march east,
without leisure to attend court.
Gradually increasing is the rock,
how numerous they are!
The mountains and rivers are long and far,
when will they end?
The warriors march east,
without leisure to return.
There is a pig with white feet,
venturing across the waves.
The moon is near the Hyades,
causing heavy rain.
The warriors march eastwards,
leaving no time for other matters.
"Jiànjiàn zhī Shí" has three stanzas,
each with six lines.
233 "Tiáo zhī Huā"
"Tiáo zhī Huā,"
is about a high official lamenting the times.
During the time of King Yōu,
the Western Róng,
and Eastern Yí tribes invaded the Central Kingdom (China) together,
armies arose everywhere,
resulting in famine and hunger.
The noble man lamented the impending fall of the Zhōu dynasty,
and grieved at encountering such times himself,
therefore he composed this poem.
The flowers of the Tiáo,
are turning yellow.
My heart is full of sorrow,
and is wounded by it.
The flowers of the Tiáo,
their leaves are green.
Knowing me to be in this state,
it would be better to have never been born!
The ewes butt their heads on the tombs,
the three stars are in the fish trap.
People can be eaten,
but few can be filled!
"Tiáo zhī Huā" has three stanzas,
each with four lines.
234 "What Grass Is Not Yellow?"
"What Grass Is Not Yellow?"
Is from the lower states, criticizing King Yōu.
The barbarians from all directions invaded together,
The central states rebelled,
Warfare did not cease,
Treating the people like birds and beasts.
Gentlemen were worried about this,
Therefore, this poem was composed.
What grass is not yellow?
What day does not pass?
What man is not going to war,
Managing affairs in all directions?
What grass is not black?
What man does not grieve?
Alas, for us conscripted men,
Alone we are treated as outcasts!
Neither rhinoceros nor tiger,
They lead us to those wild fields.
Alas, for us conscripted men,
Morning and night, we have no leisure!
A bushy fox,
Leads to those dark grasses.
There are loaded carts,
Traveling on the roads of Zhōu!

237 "Mián"
"Mián,"
The rise of King Wén,
originated from Grand Duke.
Continuous are the gourds and their vines!
The people in their beginning,
came from earthen mounds and on the Qī River.
Grand Duke Dǎnfǔ!
Making pottery kilns and digging caves,
he had not yet a house.
Grand Duke Dǎnfǔ!
Came in the morning, riding horses.
Leading [us] along the banks of the western rivers,
until beneath Mount Qí.
And with Jiāng Nǚ,
he came to plan a home.
The plains of Zhōu were rich and fertile,

There he first began to plan,

it said the time was right,
to build our houses here.
Then we comforted, then we settled,
then we measured left, then we measured right.
Then we marked the boundaries, then we regulated,
then we surveyed the fields, then we measured the acres.
From west to east,

Then they summoned the Minister of Works,
then they summoned the Minister of Instruction,
to establish houses and homes.
Their plumb lines were straight,
they contracted the wall boards for the loading,

They rammed it with a thumping sound,
they measured it with a booming sound.
They built it with a thudding sound,
they pared the wall with a rushing sound.
The hundred walls all rose up,
the great drums could not be silenced!
Then he established the outer gate,
The outer gate was strong.
Then he established the inner gate,
The inner gate was grand.
Then he established the ancestral altar,
Where the barbarian hordes were directed.
Thus, he did not extinguish their anger,
Nor did he neglect their inquiries.
The oaks and yews were uprooted,
The roads were made smooth.
The Hùn Yí barbarians retreated,

Yú Ruì offered their completed treaty,

I said there were those who were distant and those who were close,
I said there were those who came first and those who came later,
I said there were those who came running,

"Sī Qí,"

Honors the ancestor.

250 "Gōng Liú"
"Gōng Liú,"
Zhào Kāng Gōng (召康公) admonished Chéng Wáng (成王).
Chéng Wáng (成王) was about to oversee the government,
He was admonished with the affairs of the people,
Praising Gōng Liú's (公劉) generosity towards the people,
And presenting this poem.
Generous is Gōng Liú!
He did not dwell in ease and comfort.
He then marked out the fields and boundaries,
then accumulated the stores and built the granaries.
Then he wrapped up dried provisions,
in sacks and in bags.
Thinking of harmony to use his light.
Bows and arrows were stretched,
shields, spears, and axes were raised,
and so they began their journey!
Generous is Gōng Liú!
He went to survey that vast plain.
Already populous and flourishing,
already compliant, he then proclaimed [his orders],
and there were no long sighs.
Ascending, he was on the hilltops,
descending again, he was on the plains.
What did he use to transport them?
Jade and precious stones,
scabbards and belt ornaments holding knives!
Generous is Gōng Liú!
He went to those hundred springs,
gazing upon that wide plain.
He then ascended the southern hill,
and then looked at the capital.
In the fields of the capital,
at that time, they were everywhere settled,
at that time, in huts and lodges,
At this time, speech and discussions;
At this time, talk and conversations.
Truly great is Gōng Liú!
In the capital, they settled.
Dancing gracefully and orderly,
Providing mats and stools,
Having ascended, then they rested.
Then they built their settlements,
And caught pigs from the sty;
They ladled (wine) with a gourd.
They ate and they drank,
Honoring him and following him.
Truly great is Gōng Liú!
Already broad, already long,
Already sunny, then hilly,
Surveying its sunny and shady sides.
Observing its flowing springs;
Their army was thrice-deployed;
Measuring its damp plains.
Dividing the fields for grain;
Measuring its western slopes,
Bīn's dwelling was indeed vast!
Truly great is Gōng Liú!
In Bīn they built houses.
Crossing the Wèi for turmoil (conflict),
Taking whetstones and forging tools.
The foundation was then properly laid,
Where the multitude gathered and possessed,
Confined by the Yellow Ravine,
Tracing back to the Passing Ravine.
The encampments were then dense,
Ruì Jū quickly came!

Scooping from those puddles in the field,

Grave and dignified,

O affable and kind ruler!

Fènghuáng míng yǐ,
yú bǐ gāo gāng,

Běng běng qī qī,
yōng yōng jiē jiē!
Jūnzǐ zhī chē,
jì shù qiě duō.
Jūnzǐ zhī mǎ,

Shào Mù Gōng cì Lì Wáng yě.

Cherish this central kingdom,

The people are weary,

Cherish this capital city,

Thus curb the invading cruelty;

The people indeed are wearied;
